action: When you are the last wolf in a tiny endgame (3-4 alive) and are accused with hard evidence like voting records, answer the accusation directly. Reframe your past vote as a reasonable reaction to the situation, then cite a result or vote from a still-living or already-dead Town player that undercuts the accuser. Aim to win over the swing Town player; if they are not yet persuaded, shift your pitch to the accuser's inconsistencies and to the accuser as the likelier wolf.
situation: The endgame has 3-4 players left, you are the last wolf, and an unconfirmed player is pushing a case built on your voting record. A claimed Town role's result could clear the swing player and make them an ally. Information landscape: Information-rich: full public voting records, a claimed trailseer result, and a dead player's final vote are all available. These details can be used to rebut the accuser. Stakes: One vote or one night kill decides the game: winning this vote brings the wolves to parity at the next kill, while losing it eliminates the last wolf. Consensus: The room is split with no majority. Everyone is working from public vote history and one or two claimed results, and one swing player is deciding whom to believe. My position: Driving a counter-narrative to form a defensive voting coalition with the swing player. Heat: High: the accuser has laid out your voting record and tied you to a dead wolf on a key mis-elimination. Forward exposure: Answering the accuser head-on commits you to a specific story about your old vote and to a coalition with one other player. If the swing player sides with the accuser, you are voted out right away and cannot undo it. If the swing player sides with you, you can win the vote or at least split the room. Target landscape: A field of three or four: the vocal accuser citing voting records, a claimed Town role whose claim has some support (such as a cleared visit report), and possibly another claimed role. The case against you rests on past votes, evidence rather than behavior; the case against the accuser rests on behavior and on the dead players' positions. Public vs private: Privately you are the last wolf who drove the earlier kills and mis-eliminations, while publicly you pose as an innocent Town player who made an honest deduction alongside the room.

action: When you are the last wolf on a final day with three alive and the lone Town power role is deciding between you and a quiet third player, stack the case against the quiet player. Point to their abstentions and silence, and cite your own visible contribution to Town (such as a kill on a dangerous role) as proof of loyalty. Press for a decisive vote rather than a split, since a tie lets you block and kill that night.
situation: Three players remain on the final day, and the Town power role knows it was roleblocked and suspects either you or the quiet neutral player. The quiet player may abstain to protect their own win condition. Information landscape: Information-starved about the quiet player's true role, while the identity and mechanics of the Town power role are well understood. Stakes: The next elimination or night kill ends the game: a tie or abstain majority leaves the wolf alive for the night kill, but a clean vote on the wolf ends the game for the wolves. Consensus: No consensus. The Town power role is torn between two suspects, and the neutral player is protecting their own win condition. My position: Holding out against suspicion by redirecting it onto the quiet player. Heat: Extremely high: the Town power role knows a wolf has been blocking them and sees you and the quiet player as the only suspects. Forward exposure: Accusing the quiet player is a direct commitment, but with only three alive there is no later day on which to answer for it. If the vote ties or fails, you proceed to the night, where you can still win. Target landscape: Two suspects: the quiet player who abstained often and has no confirmed role or an unconfirmed neutral role, and you, who have been vocal. The case against the quiet player rests on behavior, and the evidence is thin. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the Town power role on the relevant nights, while publicly you present yourself as a loyal Town player and the quiet player as the likelier wolf.

action: When a credible investigator accusation or counterclaim is pulling the room against your wolf partner, stay out of the partner's defense: do not urge caution, vouch for them, or advocate for them. Keep your day talk short and about other players, or stay silent, so nothing visibly ties you to the partner and the room's attention stays on the duel. If you must speak, give only neutral points that would still stand if the partner flipped wolf.
situation: A claimed investigator has outed your wolf partner with a suspicious check, or a true investigator is dueling the partner's counterclaim. The room is forming an elimination consensus while you are unsuspected. Information landscape: Moderately to highly informative. There are role claims, a check report, and possibly sentinel or healer-save evidence that backs the investigator, so the town has concrete leads. Stakes: The partner is likely lost, so the wolf side's survival now depends on you staying unsuspected. Staying uncorrelated with the partner is worth more than a failed rescue that could expose you next. Consensus: The village is converging quickly on eliminating the accused partner. Its basis is the investigator's report and supporting mechanical logic from other town roles, and the room is largely ignoring pleas to slow down. My position: holding out Heat: Low to none. You are not named, but speaking up for the accused partner would put you in the spotlight. Forward exposure: Any defense of the partner is permanent on the record and becomes an associative link once the partner flips wolf, and it cannot be undone. Silence or neutral talk commits you to nothing and leaves later options open. Target landscape: The candidates are the accused wolf partner and the claimed investigator, possibly with a counterclaimer. The room is deciding on the strength of check reports and mechanical deductions, such as a healer save or ruling out other roles, rather than on behavior. Public vs private: Privately you know the accused partner is a wolf and the accusing investigator is accurate or at least credible. Publicly the room is still debating the check, and you have no suspicion on you.

action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the surviving wolf, pick the Town claimant already under scrutiny for shaky or inconsistent statements and amplify that wobble into proof of a fake claim. Cite their own words and let a confirmed Town voice such as the vigilante or trailseer lead the push, so the vote lands on them and your name stays out of it.
situation: My wolf partner has just been eliminated and I am the surviving wolf. A Town claimant stumbles while explaining what happened to their night action, giving me an opening to steer the vote onto them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role is confirmed, night tracks and watch reports have been shared, and several role claims are on the table, so a claimant's wording stands out. Stakes: With the partner gone, each Town mis-elimination moves the lone wolf closer to parity. Pushing a wrong lynch here is worth a full Town vote while the board is still uncertain. Consensus: The room is already skeptical of the stumbling claimant, and active Town voices are ready to consolidate against them. My position: Driving the accusation, then riding the consensus as it forms. Heat: None to low; I am not named as a suspect and no check or watch result points at me. Forward exposure: Pressing an accusation ties my credibility to their flip. If they turn out to be Town it is hard to retract, but it draws little attention to me while the room is already piling on. Target landscape: A claimed Town role with muddled or inconsistent statements about their night, alongside other claimants (sentinel, trailseer, vigilante) already under public scrutiny. The case rests on behavior and phrasing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know my own night actions, such as blocking this claimant, which can make their account true, yet publicly I present their clumsy wording as evidence of lying.

action: When the partner's death has just confirmed a Town claim and the room knows a chanteuse is alive, publicly agree with the confirmed Town player's read. Then frame any reported roleblock as an open puzzle by asking the blocked claimant whom they meant to target. This keeps you looking Town-engaged and moves scrutiny onto the targets they name instead of onto the surviving wolf.
situation: My wolf partner was just exposed and killed by a confirmed Town player. A Town tracker claimant reports being roleblocked, so the town knows a chanteuse is alive and is hunting for it. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead wolf's role confirms the vigilante, the trailseer reports a block, and one victim's role is concealed. Stakes: With few players left, a single split or mis-vote can carry the lone wolf toward parity. Staying unlinked to the roleblock matters more than pushing a specific target. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned behind the confirmed vigilante's read and is looking at the blocked claimant's report. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed Town read and nudging the inquiry. Heat: Low to moderate; the town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nothing yet links the block or kill to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed Town player's valid read is low risk and easy to walk back. Discussing the roleblock draws attention to night manipulation, but it makes no false role claim and commits me to nothing specific. Target landscape: A confirmed Town player (vigilante), a claimed tracker whose action was blocked, another Town claimant, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early check on record. Reads rest on shared reports, not hard evidence on any one player. Public vs private: I privately know I carried out the block and the wolf kill, while publicly I treat the roleblock as an unsolved mystery for the town to analyze.

action: When the day-1 talk centers on someone else's night result, such as a Trailseer report or a death, and nobody is questioning you, stay low-profile. Make one or two short, on-topic remarks that don't reveal what your block did or what the wolf kill did. If anyone turns toward you, switch to the explain-your-visit approach instead of staying silent.
situation: Day 1 after a night-one death. A Trailseer or other claimant has reported a result that doesn't involve me, and the town is debating mechanics while the chanteuse is unscrutinized. Information landscape: Sparse: a few unverified claims, no confirmed evil leads, and no vote record. Stakes: Early game with plenty of Town and neutral players alive, so no single day-1 move decides the game. Staying unnoticed protects the block and the pack's kill rotation for later nights. Consensus: The room is loosely aligned on discussing the tracking claim and mechanics and leaning toward abstaining. There is no firm suspect. My position: Holding out quietly, neither driving nor opposing the room. Heat: None. No living player has addressed, questioned, or accused me. Forward exposure: Speaking about the tracking claim risks leaking knowledge only a wolf would have, and a statement made now is hard to retract. A brief, low-content contribution commits me to little and avoids looking disengaged. Target landscape: No accused suspects. The room is weighing a single Trailseer claim and the mechanics around it, and any suspect choice would rest on behavior, not evidence. Public vs private: Privately I know my block and the pack's kill outcome, including a failed attack or a roleblocked player who looks like they chose to do nothing. The public is working from one unverified result and speculation, and nobody suspects me.

action: If a Trailseer or Sentinel says they saw you visit someone, answer calmly and promptly with a short explanation that fits the rules, namely that any night action is a visit. Don't stake your credibility on a specific result claim that the real role-holder could contradict. Then steer the room to weigh the tracker's report against the other claims.
situation: A player's report that they saw me visit someone on night one forces an immediate public explanation of my movement. Information landscape: Fairly rich: several night results are on the table, including a tracker report of my visit and other confirmations of visits. Stakes: It's day 1, so no elimination is at stake, but a failed cover pulls Town power roles' night attention onto me. That can cost the wolves their chanteuse and threaten the kill rotation. Consensus: The room is split over several night-one information claims and leaning toward abstaining, not toward eliminating me yet. My position: Defensive, explaining my own movement while the room leans toward abstaining. Heat: High. I'm named directly by a tracking report, and shaky logic about how visits work would add to it. Forward exposure: A hard role claim locks me into a counter-claim against the real holder and cannot be retracted. It invites scrutiny, tracking, and punitive night actions. A minimal, rule-accurate account keeps options open and can be adjusted later. Target landscape: The tracker who reported my visit, the player I blocked, and any rival claimants. The case against me rests on a tracking report, not on proven wrongdoing. Public vs private: Publicly I must explain a visit that was really my roleblock on an active role. Privately I know no result backs any claimed role, so any detailed claim is an invention that can be contradicted.

action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on a day with no hard leads or no accusation against you, join the abstain majority instead of casting a lone or wolf-paired elimination vote on a quiet, unpressured player. The vote record is public and permanent, so an outlier vote draws night attention to you and, if your partner is later exposed, ties you to them.
situation: Day 2 vote in an early, info-poor game. Nearly everyone is abstaining, and the chanteuse (alone or alongside the wolf partner) is tempted to force a mis-elimination on a quiet villager. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified investigator, sentinel or tracker claims, null or inconclusive results, a concealed body, and no confirmed flips or caught lies. Stakes: The board is early with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. A no-elimination day costs the wolves little, while a conspicuous vote record costs them a wolf's survival. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining because it lacks evidence. It wants to let investigative and watching roles gather real information first. My position: Tempted to hold out against the abstain majority. The prescription is to move with the majority instead. Heat: Low or zero heat. The chanteuse has not been accused and is not a focus of discussion, so there is no pressure that needs relieving. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote on an unaccused player is irreversible and permanently marks the voter as a non-conforming dissenter. It attracts night attention from the sigilist, serial killer or other hunters, and it links the wolves if both vote the same way. Target landscape: Abstaining with the majority versus a quiet, unaccused player with no evidence against them. The room has no guilty checks, only unverified soft clears and inconclusive results. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the wolf pack's situation and that the quiet target is not evil, while publicly the village sees no leads and favors abstaining to gather information.

action: When your wolf partner is the target of a strong, consensus-backed accusation, vote with the majority or abstain rather than casting a counter-vote against the accuser or alongside the partner. A losing vote beside an exposed wolf is permanently on record, and once the partner's role is revealed it makes you the obvious next suspect.
situation: The wolf partner is exposed by a claimed investigator or trailseer, and the town is converging on eliminating the partner. The chanteuse is tempted to back the partner and vote against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concrete guilty check or tracking sighting, competing claims, and watch or healer-save data to parse. Stakes: The partner is almost certainly lost, since the room's majority far exceeds any counter-wagon. The only real variable is whether the chanteuse survives as the remaining wolf, which depends on not being tied to the partner's votes. Consensus: A dominant majority (often 7 or more votes) is aligned against the partner, based on a concrete check or tracking result. My position: Holding out with the partner against the clear majority. The prescription is to go with the majority instead. Heat: Low direct heat on you, since the debate centers on the partner and the claimant. Heat jumps if you break from the majority to defend the partner. Forward exposure: Voting against the information-bearing claimant or beside the accused partner is irreversible. When the partner flips as a wolf, the pairing in the vote record directly links you to them, and the claimant's role may then check or target you. Target landscape: A partner under a specific, uncountered investigative or tracking claim versus the claimant, who is attacked as a fabricator. The claimant has hard evidence while the partner has only behavioral or procedural defenses. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and the accuser (the investigator or trailseer) is telling the truth, while publicly the town's consensus is forming against the partner on claims and checks.

action: If a claimed trailseer or other claimant has exposed your visit and you are under scrutiny, follow the room's consensus (abstain or join the majority) at the ballot instead of casting a lone elimination vote against the claimant. Retaliating alone confirms hostile intent toward an information role and gives the investigator, sentinel and sigilist a reason to target you that night.
situation: A claimed trailseer outed the chanteuse's night visit and the chanteuse made a shaky counterclaim, while the whole room is voting to abstain. Information landscape: Information-rich: night-one tracker reports, sentinel watch data and sigil placements give the town concrete lines of verification against the chanteuse's story. Stakes: The chanteuse is already a visible suspect. Another conspicuous act risks being the night target of several town roles, which would halve the wolf pack. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous in abstaining and wants to act on the opening tracking and watch claims before eliminating anyone. My position: Holding out as the lone dissenter. The prescription is to join the abstain consensus instead. Heat: High heat: a claimed tracker caught you visiting another player and your improvised role claim is under immediate scrutiny. Forward exposure: A solitary vote against the claimant is irreversible and brands you as hostile to the information gatherer. It leaves you isolated while the investigator, sentinel and sigilist choose night targets. Target landscape: The claimed trailseer, who is the only person who exposed you, versus abstaining with the room. The tracker's report is concrete evidence against you, and your counterclaim is unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know the claimed tracker's report about your visit is accurate and you had to improvise a cover claim, while publicly the village is weighing the tracker's claim against your shaky counterclaim.

action: Aim the block at a different player than the pack's kill target. Pick the living town role whose next result would expose a wolf: the investigator if it still has checks and suspicion is on you, otherwise the trailseer if it could follow you or the carrier. If the investigator and trailseer are both live threats, block the investigator, because a Suspicious check on you ends the wolf team.
situation: Mid-game night after Day 2 claims. Town information roles have publicly claimed, the wolves have picked a kill, and the chanteuse must choose a block target. The investigator or tracker can expose a wolf the same night. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, shared night-1 visit logs, a recorded day-2 vote, and a known night-immune lone killer. Night results are still private claims. Stakes: The wolves are still outnumbered, so a single Suspicious investigator result or a tracker linking a wolf to the victim could lose the game. The block is the only tool that can stop that result this night. Forward exposure: The block is a visit, so an unblocked trailseer following you would see it, but the result is hidden from everyone else. It can be changed freely each night. Blocking the investigator costs nothing in the open, while a redundant block on the kill target wastes the ability. Target landscape: Candidates: the claimed investigator (checks left, possibly already voting against you), the claimed trailseer or sentinel (who may have tied a wolf to a visit), the kill target, and quiet unrevealed players (likely healer or sigilist). Claims and visit logs are public, but whether they are true is unverified.

action: If you will carry the pack kill and a sigilist has claimed or is likely active, use your block on the sigilist. A blocked sigilist places nothing and makes no visit, so no sigil can strike you when you attack. If you cannot tell who the sigilist is, block the most likely candidate instead of the kill target.
situation: The chanteuse is the pack's carrier this night. A town sigilist is alive and has signaled traps, and the wolves want to kill a tracker or investigator who exposed them. Information landscape: Information-rich: day-2 claims by the trailseer, sentinel and sigilist show active town surveillance. Whether a sigil is already on a given wolf is unknown. Stakes: Dying to a sigil on the kill night loses a wolf and exposes the chanteuse. That leaves a lone illusionist against town, which is close to losing. Forward exposure: The block is a visit but it hides the sigilist's action. If the sigilist is not the one blocked, the sigil still strikes the carrier, kills you, and reveals the chanteuse. You can switch targets each night, but a death by sigil cannot be undone. Target landscape: The claimed or suspected sigilist (2 sigils, possibly already spent), the kill target (a trailseer or sentinel who exposed a wolf visit), and other town info roles. Which player holds the sigil is deduced from public claims.

action: On a blind opening night, aim the block at an active, analytical Day-1 voice who plays like an information role (investigator or trailseer). Leave quiet players to the pack kill. A block on such a player mostly cost the town its information in this cluster, and when it did not, the block still landed on a town power role.
situation: Opening night, ten alive, wolves (chanteuse and illusionist) must choose a kill and a block with no information. The chanteuse picks whom to silence among unknown town roles, a possible unblockable lone killer, and a neutral. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, deaths, votes or recorded night results, only Day-1 discussion tone to guide the choice. Stakes: Early game with the full town alive, so no single result decides the game. The block is a cheap chance to stop an investigator check or a trailseer follow before it exposes the pack, while a wasted block or a visit that gets seen costs tempo and can expose the chanteuse. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit, so a trailseer or sentinel may see the chanteuse at the target's door, and the blocked player learns they were roleblocked. The visit and the alert cannot be undone, though both stay hidden unless an info role was watching. The kill carrier is the illusionist, whose concealment hides that victim's trace but not the chanteuse's own block visit. Target landscape: Eight non-wolf players with no public claims, no votes and no night results. The only separation between them is Day-1 behavior, namely vocal, probing players versus quiet ones. The lone killer and the neutral cannot be blocked, so some blind picks will be wasted.

action: When the wolf pack's partner is dead or exposed and a confirmed lethal Town role (e.g., the vigilante) is alive, aim the pack kill at that role and use the block on the same player if you carry the kill. If you are not the carrier, block that lethal role anyway so its shot cannot land on a wolf. This removes Town's only night-kill threat without a retaliatory shot.
situation: After a wolf partner has been killed by a confirmed vigilante, the remaining wolf faces several non-wolves with a lethal Town power still live and must stop further shots at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: the vigilante's role is confirmed by its kill, the trailseer has claimed reports, and the day vote showed divided voting blocs. Stakes: The board is near endgame with few players left; one more wolf loss ends the pack's chances, so removing the single lethal Town threat decides whether the wolf survives to parity. Forward exposure: Kill plus block on the same player is invisible beyond the morning death report; the block leaves no public trace, and the commitment is irreversible but low-risk because the target dies. Target landscape: Confirmed vigilante with lethal shots (revealed by an earlier kill on a wolf), a claimed trailseer with active reports, a claimed sigilist with unused sigils, and a quiet accused player; the vigilante is confirmed by evidence, the others are claims or behavior.

action: When Town's information roles have claimed and the pack is cooperating with the illusionist, block the claimed trailseer (or whichever active tracker or watcher threatens a wolf) while the pack kills the claimed investigator, with the kill concealed if the illusionist has a use left. This cuts Town's visit-tracking and its main information source in the same night.
situation: With the real healer eliminated, the claimed investigator is unprotected and a claimed trailseer is tracking nightly visits that could expose the wolves. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles such as the healer and necromancer are confirmed, and the investigator and trailseer have public claims and results on record. Stakes: Town has lost its healer protection but still has information roles; removing the investigator while blinding the tracker for a night shifts the information balance toward the wolves before parity pressure builds. Forward exposure: Blocking shows the village only that some blocker exists, if the blocked player speaks of it; nothing ties the block to you, and you can switch block targets nightly. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, now defenseless with the healer dead; claimed trailseer actively tracking visits; claimed sigilist holding unused sigils; claims on record but not verified, with the vigilante merely suspected.

action: With three alive and one kill reaching parity, carry the pack kill yourself and aim it at the player whose night ability could stop or punish it (vigilante with a live bullet, otherwise the most dangerous remaining role). Use the Chanteuse block in the same night on the other survivor if that player has an ability that could hurt you, such as a sigilist's sigil, or on the kill target if their shot could hit you. This leaves the town unable to answer, and the kill ends the game at parity.
situation: Endgame with three players left: the lone wolf (the Chanteuse) and two others. A single night kill reaches wolf parity once the lone killer is gone. A surviving Town player's night ability, such as a vigilante shot or a sigil, is the only thing that could punish or stop the wolf. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles are revealed, the lone killer or other threats are eliminated, and the survivors' roles and remaining abilities are known from claims and deduction. Stakes: The next night's kill decides the game. One successful kill ends it in a wolf win, while a failed or retaliated kill hands the town a chance to turn it around. Neutralizing any threat to the Chanteuse is the priority. Forward exposure: Irreversible and game-ending: the kill resolves into 1-on-1 parity, so there is no later daytime exposure. The block is a visit but is only seen by the blocked player, who is told they were roleblocked. Target landscape: Two living non-wolf targets, both with publicly known or claimed roles. One holds a lethal or punishing night ability (a vigilante with unused bullets, or a sigilist with sigils left). The other is exhausted or passive (a sentinel with no watches left, a trailseer, or a coasting neutral). Reads are based on confirmed claims and elimination.

action: With zero heat and no role claim of your own, stay in the analytical middle: restate what each investigative claimant reported, ask the accused to explain their visits, and point out which claims conflict. Hold back from committing to one target until the explanations come in, so you stay a low-profile voter while the village's own evidence does the work.
situation: A day discussion in which night deaths have produced visit reports from claimed trailseer or sentinel players. Those reports point at an accused player or create competing leads, and the fortune teller has no heat and is still working toward two prediction points. Information landscape: Mixed but mostly information-rich: announced deaths and roles, plus claimed visit reports that conflict or are contested. Reports are claims, not announcements, so they can be checked against how the rules treat concealed victims. Stakes: The board is mid-game and not at the brink; one wrong day-vote hurts Town but does not end the game. The fortune teller's own win depends on surviving nights to score points, so staying unnoticed matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: The room is engaged and fairly aligned on dissecting the visit reports. There is no firm lean yet, or it is forming around the accused visitor. It rests on claimed results rather than announced facts. My position: With the majority, not driving. Contributing a summary but taking no hard stance. Heat: None. No one is suspecting or questioning the fortune teller, who is a neutral with no side and reads Not suspicious. Target landscape: Several living players with unverified role claims and visit reports from a claimed trailseer or sentinel; the accused deny or counter-claim. The basis is claimed night results and explanations, not confirmed facts.

action: When the day opens with little evidence and just one or two claims, agree with the claim and add one modest logical observation, such as which roles a given report cannot cover. Then let others speak, without proposing a target, so the discussion stays calm and you stay unnoticed.
situation: An early day after a night kill, with no wolf-kill leads or checks revealed. One investigative claimant has reported a non-visit result and the village is just starting to interpret night movements. Information landscape: Information-starved: a single dead player and one claimed no-visit result, with no investigative checks, caught lies or voting record to go on. Stakes: Early game with plenty of cushion; no single vote or kill flips the game. The aim is to stay alive for more night bets while adding no suspicion, since there is little to gain from pushing a read now. Consensus: Calm and undirected. Players echo each other's observations, with no accusation forming and a leaning toward abstaining. My position: With the majority. Echoing and refining shared observations, not driving. Heat: None. No one has voiced suspicion of the fortune teller. Target landscape: A claimed trailseer or similar reporter clears one quiet player. The other living players have unknown roles and no concrete leads, so there is no basis yet for a behavioral accusation.

action: When the room has already stacked elimination votes on you, cast your vote on the other leading suspect, the player with the least verified role or night results. An abstention lowers no one's count and can't force a tie, while a vote on the rival adds to a split or tie that could leave no one eliminated, and it pressures a plausible lone killer or wolf. If the votes against you are already a locked majority, the vote still goes to the rival rather than to nobody.
situation: Late in the game, the town's power roles are mostly confirmed or consistent with each other. The vote has narrowed to me versus one other unverified player, and I must choose between abstaining and voting the rival. Information landscape: Info-rich: role claims cover the town slots, saves and night results corroborate the town roles, and the public voting record is visible. The only open question is who among the unverified players is the lone killer or a wolf. Stakes: With few players left, one elimination changes the balance of power. My death ends my scoring chances, since a day vote never scores, so I must use my vote to split the count or push the real threat out. Consensus: The village is largely unified, on role-claim bookkeeping and corroborated night results, that the leftover unverified players are the problem. Neutral is treated as expendable. My position: holding out Heat: Extreme: several players, including confirmed town power roles, have declared votes against me because I am an expendable neutral once the town slots are claimed or corroborated. Target landscape: Two or three unverified players: me, an outed neutral fortune teller, and a rival with an unverified or contested claim (e.g. a vigilante or sentinel claimant suspected of being the lone killer). Every other living player holds a role corroborated by night events. The basis is process of elimination, not hard evidence on the rival.

action: When the room dogpiles a quiet, unvetted player with no concrete evidence, don't join the pile. Abstain if abstaining is offered, or vote for the counter-suspect who has actual evidence against them. A dead Town power role with unused bullets or abilities can be used by a Necromancer through its body, which could cost you the nights you need to score.
situation: After a night death, such as a wolf shot down by a sigil, the town dogpiles an unconfirmed player at the vote instead of vetting claims. If the victim turns out to be a Town power role, the body is exposed to a Necromancer. Information landscape: Some roles are confirmed from dead bodies and some visits are verified, but there is no hard evidence on the vote candidates. Most of the reads are speculative. Stakes: The board is mid-game with several evil factions still alive. A wrong elimination of a power role gives the lone killer a weapon and costs the fortune teller nights, so it is a costly vote even though it does not end the game. Consensus: The village converges suddenly on one quiet player after a night death, without demanding claims or weighing conflicting accusations. The agreement rests on behavior and momentum, not evidence. My position: Following the majority, with no independent read on the target. Heat: Negligible. The fortune teller is not a suspect and is not drawing accusations. Target landscape: Two or more unvetted players, one quiet with no stated role and one accused by others. There are no investigative results on either, and the push against the quiet player comes from momentum after a death rather than evidence.

action: Before voting, count your points. If you have fewer than two and the leading candidate is a wolf whose removal would leave Town one elimination from winning, abstain if it is offered. If abstaining is not offered, vote for the least-supported candidate who is not a confirmed evil player, so the game runs long enough for your bets to score. A Town win ends the game before you can reach two points.
situation: The village is about to eliminate a wolf in an information-rich endgame where only one wolf would remain. Town can then win at night through a sigil strike or another kill. The fortune teller has not yet scored its second point. Information landscape: Rich. There is a prior Serial Killer elimination, night-one tracking testimony, and a sigil result, but no certainty about which evil is left. Stakes: Town is close to a win. One more evil removal leaves a lone wolf who can be killed that same night, and the game ends before the fortune teller scores. Your vote helps decide whether the game continues. Consensus: The village is building a majority against the tracked suspect on the strength of testimony and arguments. The agreement is moderately solid. My position: Aligned with the forming majority and reinforcing the case, which makes you a driver of the elimination. Heat: Low overall. The accused player may cast an isolated retaliatory vote at you, but the room is not suspicious of you. Target landscape: A suspected wolf, tracked or accused with an inconclusive sigil test, plus a claimed role under pressure from a quiet player. The suspected wolf is the main case, backed by daytime arguments and a Trailseer's testimony but no hard confirmation.

action: With both self-bets still unspent and no points scored, bet on the player the killers most plausibly want dead tonight: an openly active, publicly claimed information role (such as a trailseer that just exposed someone) or a player the dead Trailseer's last follow pointed to. Name no role, since the death alone scores a point, and keep the self-bets for later nights.
situation: Early game (night 1 or 2), the Fortune Teller has no points yet and must pick a nightly death bet while wolves and a lone killer are all hunting. Day discussion produced a visible conflict or a prominent claimed power role. Information landscape: Mixed: some claims and night-one movement reports exist, but roles are unverified and votes were mostly abstentions, so the pick rests on behavioral reads. Stakes: No immediate parity pressure. The Fortune Teller needs two points in total, so each night's bet is a cheap, repeatable chance to score, and the self-bets guard against a later attack. Target landscape: Players who publicly claimed or acted as information roles, or who were just singled out by a night result or an open dispute, versus quiet players with no evidence either way. The choice rests on behavioral threat to the killers, not confirmed alignment.

action: On a night with no evidence at all (no claims, no deaths, no votes), bet on any one quiet living player without naming a role, since the bet scores on any death by any cause. Keep both self-bets unspent for later nights when you may become a target.
situation: Night one after a discussion-only opening day. Several killers (wolves, and possibly a lone killer) will each attack someone, and no public mechanical constraint limits their choices. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigative findings, deaths, confirmed roles, or vote record exist. Stakes: Very low board pressure. A miss costs nothing but a night, and multiple attackers raise the chance that the chosen player dies. A hit on night one puts the win one successful bet away. Target landscape: All other living players, with no public claims, revealed alignments, or voting history to separate them. Any pick is close to a random draw among the candidates.

action: With three alive and a night kill that is predictable (a publicly confirmed Town role whose own actions are blocked or spent, with a wolf free to carry the kill), bet on that player to die and name their confirmed role. A correct victim plus role scores two points and can finish the win.
situation: Three-player endgame tie between a confirmed Town power role, a suspected wolf and the Fortune Teller. The wolves need a kill to close the game, and the Fortune Teller needs points to win. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles are confirmed by earlier night results and blocked actions, so the wolves' likely victim can be read from the board. Stakes: Each night is nearly decisive. A correct victim-and-role bet gives two points and wins the game for the Fortune Teller, while a miss wastes a night when the kill can end the game. Target landscape: A publicly confirmed Town role (e.g. a claimed vigilante whose shots were blocked), a suspected surviving wolf, or a self-bet. The Town player is the most likely kill target, backed by confirmed evidence from earlier nights and blocks rather than just behavior.

action: With three alive and a lone killer that can attack, you are one of only two possible victims. If no other victim is predictable, spend a self-bet, because an attack on you fails that night. Don't bet on the suspected killer: a killer that is immune or about to win is unlikely to die, and a wrong bet leaves you open to the attack.
situation: Last wolf voted out and three players left. A lone killer (the necromancer, who can attack through a reanimated body) wins by killing one more player, so the Fortune Teller is a live kill target and no other player's death is predictable. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves are dead, the dead roles are confirmed, and the remaining Town sigilist is confirmed out of sigils. This makes the only remaining attacker and its available bodies clear. Stakes: The lone killer wins if anyone else dies tonight, so a bet that fails to cover your own life can end the game with the Fortune Teller short of two points. A self-bet keeps you alive for another night. Target landscape: The suspected necromancer (alive and holding a usable body, so unlikely to die), a confirmed sigilist with no sigils left (no threat), or a self-bet. Roles are confirmed from the graveyard, and nothing makes the suspect likely to die tonight.

action: When the healer has publicly announced protecting the obvious top target (the confirmed or claimed investigator), place the bet on the next-most-valuable unshielded Town role the surviving killer must remove, such as the claimed healer or another power role. If the killer's last pick is predictable, name that role in the bet for the two-point payoff.
situation: Late game with the wolves dead or nearly dead and one killer left (serial killer, necromancer or last wolf). The Fortune Teller stands at 0-1 points and needs a death, and the most obvious target is publicly protected, so a bet on them fails to the save or the killer switches targets. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of the dead wolves are confirmed, claims and protection histories are public, and the surviving killer's identity or kill pattern is mostly known. Stakes: Few players remain and the game can end any night. Each night spent without scoring risks being voted out or the game finishing before the second point, so the bet must follow where the killer can actually kill, not just where it wants to. Target landscape: The investigator or leader shielded by a public healer claim, the claimed healer who is exposed, other claimed power roles (sigilist, sentinel, trailseer), and unconfirmed players. Hard evidence of who is protected, not behavior, drives the choice.

action: When one killer remains and a claimed power role has just driven the day's outcome (outed a wolf, tested the wolf, or led the vote), bet on that role as the killer's top threat, not on the accused or already-exposed suspect. A killer that is under suspicion usually survives the night, and the threat to it is the likelier victim.
situation: After a day elimination or accusation, the remaining killer needs to silence the player who exposed it or holds a deadly tool against it. The Fortune Teller must choose between betting on the accused (who survives) and betting on the exposing claimant (who is attacked). Information landscape: Information-rich: a public claim or result (tracker report, sigil test, investigator checks) points at the killer's side, and several Town roles are out in the open. Stakes: Only one killing source is left, so exactly one death is likely each night and the bet must match it. A miss leaves the Fortune Teller stuck at one point while the game may end that same night. Target landscape: The claimed tracker, sigilist or investigator who exposed or tested the killer's side, versus the accused wolf or suspect, versus bystander claimed roles such as a roleblocked sentinel or unconfirmed healer. The basis is public claims and the day's vote record.

action: When a protected player's survival has been announced as a save and you decide to claim healer, confirm the save and then stop. Do not announce which player you will protect next; if asked, say only that you will keep protecting where it helps. This keeps the lone killer from reading your protection pattern, and a claim made while the room still has other confirmed town roles (e.g. a trailseer) lets your death be turned into information.
situation: After an announced healer save on a claimed town role, late in the game with the wolves dead and a lone killer remaining, the healer decides whether and how to claim and what to say about future protection. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves are dead and revealed, saves have been announced, and several town roles are confirmed or consistent. Only the lone killer's identity is unresolved. Stakes: With few players left, losing the healer removes the only protection and brings the lone killer close to parity. The healer's death is likely after a claim, so the claim should leave the town better placed to catch the killer and should not hand over the targeting information for free. Consensus: The village is aligned and trusting: saves were announced, wolves are dead, and the room is narrowing suspects among the unclaimed players. My position: driving Heat: No suspicion of being evil, since the save report backs the claim. Heat as a night-kill target rises sharply once the role is public. Forward exposure: Claiming healer is irreversible and makes the non-self-protecting healer an obvious night target for the lone killer. Announcing the next protection target adds a further commitment that the killer can exploit; withholding it is fully reversible. Target landscape: Few unconfirmed players remain, with most town roles accounted for and the wolves dead. The remaining evil is a lone killer (necromancer or serial killer) hiding among the unclaimed or unverified seats, judged on claims and night-result evidence. Public vs private: Publicly the town only knows that a save occurred; privately the healer knows exactly whom they protected and on which nights. Revealing the role is confirmed by the announcement, but stating the future target would hand the killer new information.

action: If a Sentinel report places you at a target's door and the room is converging on you, claim Healer and tie the visit to the game-master-announced saves to break the suspicion. Accept that the wolves will target you next, and make the claim only when the vote threat is real.
situation: A Sentinel report places the healer among the visitors at a claimed investigator's door, next to a rival claimant and a dead player, and the village is leaning toward voting out a visitor. Information landscape: Information-rich from the Sentinel's multiple visits, though clouded by reanimation mechanics. Stakes: A vote on a visitor could remove the healer or push the town into a tied vote. The claim removes the immediate vote threat at the cost of the wolves' attention. Consensus: The room treats the visitors named in the Sentinel's report as the main suspects. The vote is leaning toward them and could tie. My position: holding out Heat: High at first, because you are named as a visitor to the primary target. It drops once the role claim ties the visit to the announced saves. Forward exposure: The claim is irreversible and maximal: it permanently marks you as the healer to the wolves, and a kill on you is likely the next night. It does clear the visit explanation at once. Target landscape: You and a rival visitor claimant, both under suspicion from the Sentinel's report, against quiet players with no evidence on them. The basis is visit evidence rather than behavior. Public vs private: Publicly you are a living visitor in a visit report, one suspect among several; privately you know the visit was your protection.

action: When the room is busy with hard evidence (an investigator result, a watcher or follower catch, a counterclaim) and nobody is questioning you, stay unclaimed and add only sincere public-board reasoning that backs the credible lead, e.g. 'wolves attacked the investigator claimant, so a wolf-conspiracy accusation doesn't hold'. This keeps the village consolidated while your role and protection target stay hidden, so the evil sides cannot aim kills or blocks at you.
situation: After a morning report with an announced save or visit catches, the room fights over an accused player versus a claimant with a result. The healer is unclaimed and unsuspected, and the evidence points toward the claimant being genuine. Information landscape: Information-rich: a game-master-announced attack and save, claimed investigator results, visit reports from the sentinel or trailseer, and a revealed dead role. Stakes: Mid-game with no immediate parity threat. The healer's long-term protective value matters more than any single vote, so staying anonymous preserves the town's strongest repeatable defensive resource. Consensus: The village is organizing around one confrontation and credible evidence such as a guilty check or a visit catch, with little friction. My position: with majority Heat: Zero. Nobody has addressed or questioned the healer, who is a background participant. Forward exposure: Speaking from public facts commits the healer to nothing and is fully reversible, so the role stays anonymous. Claiming Healer would be irreversible and would expose the role to night kills and blocks. Target landscape: Players already in the spotlight: a claimed investigator with a guilty check against an accused dissenter, or a caught visitor with a counterclaim. They are judged on evidence (checks, visit reports, announced saves) rather than on behavior. Public vs private: The public knows only an announced save or a set of claimed results; privately the healer knows their own protection choice and whether it matches the announcement, and so can judge the claimant more confidently than others, but has no need to reveal it.

action: If an announced save on a player is followed by contested claims for a unique role, or by the room stalling over who to trust, and your own protection on that player was real, claim Healer and confirm you protected them. This turns the announcement into an anchor so the village can focus on the false claimant. Do this only when the anchor is worth more than losing anonymity, and expect the evil roles to target you with blocks or kills afterwards.
situation: The Game Master announced an attack and a save on a player. At the same time, two players claim the same unique role, and the village lacks a trusted anchor to resolve the conflict. Information landscape: Information-rich in announcements (a system-confirmed save) but contested in claims. One of the two claimants must be lying, and nothing verifies either of them. Stakes: A wrong lean on the counterclaim could cost a key town role or hand evil tempo. The healer's confirmation can decide which claimant the village believes, at the price of becoming the primary night-kill and block target. Consensus: The village is unsettled and split between two competing claims, and wants a verifiable fact to orient around. My position: driving Heat: Low. The healer's earlier actions were cross-verified or unquestioned, so no suspicion attaches to them. Forward exposure: Claiming Healer is irreversible and exposes the role to roleblocks and night attacks from evil roles, but it buys maximum credibility because it matches a Game Master announcement. Target landscape: Two counter-claimants for a single unique role slot, with one lying. The saved player's protection is verifiable from the announcement, while the claimants are judged on claims alone. Public vs private: The Game Master announced that a specific player was attacked and saved. Privately the healer knows they chose to protect that player, so the claim would verify the public report.

action: If another player claims the Healer credit for a save you made, counterclaim in that same discussion. Name the night and the player you protected, and ask the village to compare the two accounts, instead of staying quiet and waiting.
situation: A watcher's report shows two visitors at the saved player's door. The other visitor immediately claims Healer and takes credit for the save while I say nothing about my role. Information landscape: Information-rich: formal Investigator and Trailseer results and a Sentinel-style visit report give a checkable timeline. Role claims on that timeline are still unverified. Stakes: If a wolf's fake Healer claim sticks, the town loses its protector and the wolves gain a trusted voice. A vote swing, or my own elimination, can decide the game. Consensus: The village is unanimous against another suspect and is accepting the rival Healer claim without challenge. My position: With the majority on the target, but silent on a role claim that I should contest. Heat: Moderate. I was named as a visitor to the saved player, though the room is currently looking at someone else. Forward exposure: Counterclaiming reveals me as the Healer and makes me a night-kill target. Staying silent concedes the claim space to a liar and is harder to reverse, because a late counterclaim reads as a reaction and gets rejected. Target landscape: The candidates are the rival Healer claimant, a watcher exposed by door-traffic information, and myself, a known visitor to the saved player's door. The basis is claimed visit lists and the first claim to be made, not verified facts. Public vs private: I know I made the protection and that the rival claimant is lying, but the public sees only a plausible Healer claim and me as an ambiguous visitor. Every silent turn lets the false claim gain credibility.

action: When confirmed roles and the tracking or vote record leave one clear suspect, vote for that suspect with the majority. If instead you are on a counter-wagon against a rival claimant, vote to eliminate that rival to stay alive, because a living healer who keeps protecting is worth more to Town than leaving the room unresolved.
situation: Mid-to-late game with few players alive, wolves partly or mostly dead, and a day vote where a suspect deflects with a weak argument, or a lone killer backs a rival claimant's push against me. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles are revealed, a night tracking result and a kill record exist, and several roles are confirmed or claimed, which narrows the hidden evil roles. Stakes: With about five to six alive and evil roles still hidden, each vote moves the board toward parity or toward a win. Losing the healer or letting a wolf live shortens the game, so the vote must remove a probable evil player or save me. Consensus: The village is partly aligned around the evidence trail, and in the late game a hidden evil player may push a rival wagon. My position: with majority Heat: Ranges from none to two locked votes against me. When a counter-wagon exists, it is built on a claim that mine is fabricated. Forward exposure: A vote is public and permanent but reveals nothing about my role. Voting with the evidence or the majority adds no exposure, while voting against a rival claimant commits me to that read and cannot be undone. Target landscape: Candidates are the player named by the tracking trail or the failed deflection, a claimed sigilist or other claimant whose abilities are spent, and analytical voices who may be the target of counter-accusations. The basis is mostly hard evidence (tracking result, dead roles, confirmed kills) plus behavior. Public vs private: Privately I know I am the healer and what my protections did. Publicly the room judges claims and tracking trails with no proof of my role, and sometimes a rival claim attacks my credibility.

action: Each night, choose the protect target from who the remaining killer is likely to attack, not from who held the most value yesterday. A claimed investigator who just exposed a wolf is the likely kill, so protect them. If your protection plan is public or has been repeated for several nights, expect the killer to route around it and switch to another valuable town role.
situation: All or nearly all wolves are dead and a lone killer (serial killer or necromancer) is the main night threat. The healer must pick a protect target among the claimed town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolf roles are revealed, claims are on the floor, and the investigator's results are public. The killer's identity and next target are still unknown. Stakes: With about five players alive and one lone killer left, each night kill is a large loss. A wasted protection or a lost healer shifts the numbers toward the killer, so the protect choice carries real weight. Target landscape: Claimed investigator (high historical value, recent wolf-exposer or checks spent), other claimed utility roles (trailseer, sigilist, sentinel), and quiet unclaimed players; judged by public claims and recent day behavior, with no night evidence.

action: If you have publicly named your protect target, or have guarded the same player for consecutive nights, change targets. A killer who reads the pattern can skip the guarded player and attack you or an unguarded role, so an unpredictable pick keeps both your protection and your own life in play. Skip a target whose ability is spent or whose threat is gone (a sentinel with no watches, an investigator with no checks), and guard the live information role the killer most wants removed.
situation: The healer has repeated the same protection across nights or announced it publicly, and the claimed target's ability is spent or its threat to the killer has faded. The killer can avoid the telegraphed target and hit the healer or an active role instead. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles are publicly claimed, and spent abilities (sentinel watches, investigator checks) have been stated openly. The killer's choices are visible only through morning outcomes. Stakes: Losing the healer, or an active investigator, with one killer left lets the killer avoid saves from then on. A predictable protection pattern risks giving up the night's save and the healer itself. Target landscape: The previously protected player (claimed investigator or spent sentinel) versus other live claimed utility roles with active abilities; assessed from public claims about spent abilities and from the killer's past target choices.

action: When the board is information-rich and a publicly confirmed Town power role (e.g. a validated Investigator whose result was corroborated by a death) is the obvious priority kill, protect that player again even if the pick feels predictable. Both the wolves and a lone killer have reason to remove them, so a repeat guard can stop two attacks in one night. If the evidence instead points to a different Town power role as the likelier target, switch to that player.
situation: After an evil player's death corroborated a Town power role's results, both killing factions have a strong incentive to remove that role. The Healer picks tonight's protection among the visible Town power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead evil players are confirmed, a Town power role's check was corroborated, voting records are public, and several Town roles are openly known. Stakes: The board is mid-game with evil still holding a kill. Losing the validated power role would cost Town its best information source, while a successful save denies evil a kill and keeps Town numbers up. Target landscape: Confirmed Town power roles (a validated Investigator, a claimed Sentinel, a claimed Sigilist) plus a few unrevealed players. The Investigator's checks are corroborated by a dead evil player, so the choice rests on evidence rather than behavior alone.

action: After the Serial Killer is voted out and several Town info roles have publicly claimed, protect the claimed role whose verified result is doing the most damage to the wolves (the one that caught the killer or placed a wolf at a kill scene). Wolves tend to silence the most active public information source, so put the protection there rather than on a secondary claim, even one that just won a counter-claim dispute.
situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote on the strength of tracking and watch results. Wolves still hold the night kill, and the healer must choose among multiple publicly claimed Town power roles to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated, tracking and watch results produced verified visits, and role claims and counter-claims are on the record. Stakes: Wolves are still alive, with Town ahead on numbers. Losing the lead information role would blunt Town's momentum, so a correct protection preserves the lead while a wrong one costs the best tracker and leaves wolves freer. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed Town power roles (a Trailseer who caught a visit, a Sentinel who exposed the Serial Killer, a Sigilist or Investigator with softer results) and quiet players. The claims rest on verified night visits and the exposed killer, not just behavior, and the ranking depends on whose result most threatens the wolves.

action: On the night after a claimed investigator, sentinel or other information role has become the town's most visible information source, protect that claimant, since the wolves most likely attack the player who is verified or clearing others. If two claimants compete, protect the one whose results are most useful to the town (an investigator who has cleared you, or one whose check was confirmed by an elimination) over a less-pressing claimant.
situation: Early night (night 2) after a public information-role claim, with the wolves (and possibly a lone killer) choosing their kill and the town's key information source an obvious target. Information landscape: Mostly unverified claims with few or no confirmed flips or wills, sometimes partly confirmed by a correct elimination; the claimant's visibility is the main evidence, and the healer has no hard read on which claim is real. Stakes: Losing the lead information role this early strips the town of checks before any roles are confirmed, while a save wastes the wolves' kill and keeps the town's lead intact; the board is not yet at parity, so one lost key role hurts but is not decisive. Target landscape: Several claimed information roles (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) and quiet unclaimed players; the investigator who cleared the healer or whose check was validated is the most prominent unverified-or-confirmed target, versus a sentinel or trailseer with less impact.

action: If your protected target survived an attack last night and remains the town's key confirmed information role or leader, protect them again, because wolves usually persist against the most threatening claimant. Switch the protection only if new evidence shows the wolves have moved to a different, more valuable target.
situation: The previous night's protected key claimant was attacked and saved, and the town debates whether the wolves will repeat the attack or hunt elsewhere, possibly with an impostor claiming credit for the save. Information landscape: Information-rich: a public save announcement, an eliminated wolf or necromancer role revealed, and known claims about visitors; the healer knows their own protection record, others only have claims. Stakes: Two consecutive successful saves deny the wolves back-to-back kills, preserving the town's majority and its leading voice; wasting the night on a lower-value target risks losing the key claimant for no gain. Target landscape: The confirmed or leading investigator who just survived an attack, versus other claimants (sigilist, sentinel) and quiet players with no sign of being targeted; the investigator's survival and wolf persistence are the basis, not behavior reads.

action: On a blind opening night, protect one engaged, neutral-baseline player rather than stalling over the choice, since there is no evidence to rank candidates and you cannot protect yourself. Treat the night as a free baseline visit: if the morning shows a save or a death, that is the first real data for choosing Night 2 targets.
situation: Opening night after a discussion-only Day 1. The healer must pick a protect target for the pack's first kill with no prior results, and the wolves may kill the healer instead. Information landscape: Information-starved: no deaths, no checks, no votes and no claims, only brief introductory remarks. Stakes: Early game with a full board, so a single night's protection will not decide the game. Losing the healer early removes protection from Night 2 onward, but the blind target cannot be improved with the information available. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public claims, no verified roles and no vote record. The only basis is thin Day 1 behavior, so the pick is speculative.

action: When you are publicly exposed and expect to be attacked, spend the night protecting the claimed power role that has shown real value or already drawn an attack, such as a sentinel you protected before while a necromancer is striking through bodies. Keep that player covered on consecutive nights if the attacker's pattern still points at them, because a save blanks the strike and keeps their ability in play even if you die afterward.
situation: Mid-game, after a confirmed wolf elimination. The healer has publicly revealed their role and prior protection and is likely the next kill. A necromancer is also active and attacking through dead bodies. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed illusionist elimination validated the trailseer's report, and the morning announcements show an active necromancer attacking through bodies. Stakes: Late-mid game with few players left, so each save or loss shifts the balance sharply. Keeping a power role alive through a strike matters even though the exposed healer will probably die that night. Target landscape: Other living players, mainly two claimed power roles (a sentinel you previously protected and a trailseer whose report just led to an elimination). Both have public standing, and the choice rests on the attack pattern and prior protection rather than certainty.

action: When a claimed night result (a visit report, zero-visit report, or clearing) touches you or your wolf partner on day 1 or 2, endorse the result or a verification step in cautious town-sounding language, and agree with any caveat another player raises. Do not hard-claim a role or deny a visit that a claim could contradict; stay with the majority drift toward abstain.
situation: Early in the game a claimed investigative or tracking result (visit report, zero-visit report, or clearing) touches the illusionist or its wolf partner. The village is deciding whether to act on it or to abstain. Information landscape: Information-starved: several unverified claims, no deaths or engine reports that confirm any alignment, and the key facts are one player's word against another's. Stakes: Early game with many players alive, so one wolf exposure would be costly but no single vote decides the game. Keeping the pack unquestioned and reaching an abstain preserves the wolves' numbers for later parity. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned on caution with no firm accusation, and is drifting toward an abstain because nothing can be verified. My position: with majority Heat: Low to moderate: named in a claimed visit or warned about, but shielded by overlapping claims or the lack of a firm accusation. Forward exposure: Endorsing or suggesting verification commits the illusionist only to sounding cautious and cooperative, and it can be walked back. A flat denial or a hard role claim would be much harder to reverse if a watcher or follower contradicts it. Target landscape: The claimants (tracker, sentinel, trailseer, investigator) are unverified. The wolf partner or the illusionist is the named subject of the claims, and no one is yet accused on hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the wolves' night activity (the carrier's kill, a block, or a hidden visit) and how it relates to the claimed result. Publicly the table reads the claims as benign or unverifiable and is debating whether they are fiction or simply odd.

action: When a claimed watch or tracking result names your partner or you as a visitor, acknowledge only the visit that cannot be disproved. Frame it as a casual check-in and point the room at the strangest part of the data, such as several players visiting the same target. This keeps your claim consistent with the visits other players can report while avoiding a specific role claim.
situation: A sentinel or trailseer publicly lists the illusionist among several visitors to one player, creating a risk of an investigation trap. Information landscape: Fairly rich in visit data from several claimed watchers, but nothing is verified by deaths and the data converges on an odd target. Stakes: A single named-visitor result could expose the pack on day 2; defusing it keeps both wolves alive and the vote at abstain. Consensus: The village treats the multi-visit pile-up as a puzzle and has no single suspect, so it leans toward abstaining. My position: with majority Heat: Moderate: explicitly named by a sentinel as a visitor, diluted by other claimants reporting the same visits. Forward exposure: Admitting a visit commits the illusionist to being a visiting role in later claims, and it is only partly reversible. Avoiding a specific role claim keeps flexibility. Target landscape: The quiet visited player and the other visitors defending their own overlapping actions. All are unverified claimants, and the evidence is visit lists rather than behavior. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the visit was the wolf kill or another wolf action, whereas the town sees an inexplicable convergence of visits on one quiet player.

action: When your wolf partner is already dead and a claimed sentinel or other watcher accuses an outside killer, back the watcher's report and press the accused to explain their visit. This helps the town remove the lone killer without any suspicion falling on you. Keep your wording the same as the rest of the village's.
situation: A claimed watcher reports a visitor at the dead wolf partner's door, and the accused denies it while the village weighs the two stories. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed dead wolf, a watcher's claim about its visitors, and a supporting investigator result. Stakes: Removing the lone killer is necessary before wolves can win and costs the pack nothing, while staying unscrutinized keeps the illusionist alive for the endgame. Consensus: Town converges on the accused and the vote is nearly unanimous. My position: with majority Heat: None: no one has linked the illusionist to the kill or questioned its behavior. Forward exposure: Backing the watcher commits the illusionist to treating that claimant as credible later, though that is easy to revisit if the watcher is contradicted. Target landscape: The accused visitor, who claims town and denies the visit, versus the claimed watcher whose report is plausible given the dead wolf. The basis is a watch result, not behavior. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows its partner was killed by an outside night killer, so the accused visitor is probably that killer, and the public read matches this.

action: When an unverified watcher or follower reports your visit at a victim's or target's door and you are exposed, immediately claim a Town role whose action explains that visit (e.g. Healer protecting the target), and tie it to the night's outcome. If the claim fits the report and the room accepts it, steer the town toward the player who raised the report, and plan the later collision with the real role-holder.
situation: A claimed watcher or tracker reports visits to a player who survived or died, and I (a wolf-side illusionist) am among the visitors named or about to be exposed. Information landscape: Information-rich: visit reports, an attack that was thwarted or a body, and several role claims on the table, though none verified. Stakes: Mid-game with a wolf exposed by a visit report; a single failed explanation risks a vote on me, while a convincing cover keeps the wolf pack on course toward parity. Consensus: The room is information-rich and willing to act on visit reports, but has not settled on who is lying; it accepts any claim that plausibly explains the visits. My position: Driving; I set the narrative right after the report by claiming first and redirecting focus. Heat: High; named as a visitor at a sensitive door by a claimed night-information role on the exact night of the event. Forward exposure: A fake role claim locks me in publicly and guarantees a collision if the genuine role-holder is alive; it is hard to retract, but it buys immediate safety and can set up removing the real role-holder. Target landscape: The unverified observer who reported visits, the genuine role-holder whose action matches my claim, and the surviving target; the observer's claim is unverified while my cover story is plausible. Public vs private: Privately I know the visit was a wolf action (kill attempt or ability use), but publicly the visit must be framed as a Town role's action to explain being seen.

action: When a claimed tracker or watcher reports you at a victim's door, do not rely on a bare denial: pair it with a coherent counter-story, such as a plausible role claim with a believable alibi. Use any competing role conflict in the room to draw attention off yourself, but keep the counter-story ready so the report cannot resurface later.
situation: A claiming tracker names me as a visitor to the night-one victim while a separate dual-claim conflict dominates the room. Information landscape: Information-rich: two investigative claims with direct visit reports on both night deaths, plus a hard counterclaim. Stakes: A named wolf-side visitor who survives today by deflection but leaves the accusation unresolved; it can return at the next vote and cost a wolf while the pack still needs several eliminations. Consensus: The room is split and distracted by a bigger role-claim dispute, so it can be redirected but has not cleared me. My position: With majority; I am following the room's focus on the other conflict while deflecting from my own accusation. Heat: High; named by a claimed tracker as a visitor to the night victim, though partly diluted by another player caught at a different body. Forward exposure: A flat denial commits me to calling the reporter a liar without any role alibi; it is reversible only by building a story later, and if the reporter survives or is validated it brings me down. Target landscape: The claiming tracker who named me, a rival dispute (conflicting claims of the same role) in the room, and myself; the reports are unverified but the tracker's claim is accurate. Public vs private: Privately I know the report is accurate because I carried out the kill, while publicly the room is split over a different dispute and can be pointed away from me.

action: When your wolf partner is dead and revealed and the room is tying you to their Day 2 vote, explain that vote as an ordinary standalone read and anchor it in a different, plausible suspect. Then steer the room toward a third party, such as a quiet non-wolf with no confirmed role, rather than attacking the claimed investigator whose result already matches the revealed role. Attacking a claim the death record has already confirmed only draws attention to the voting record.
situation: Your wolf partner has been killed and revealed. A claimed investigator or other Town claimants are pointing at your matching vote history and pressing you as the second wolf. Information landscape: Information-rich: a revealed wolf role, a concealed or confirmed kill, claimed investigative results that line up with the death record, and a permanent Day 2 voting record. Stakes: With the partner gone and few players left, the Illusionist is the last wolf. Being voted out ends the wolf team, and surviving a day keeps the team alive toward parity. Consensus: The village is converging on you because the voting record links you to the revealed wolf. Any claimed result that matches the revealed role strengthens that convergence. My position: holding out Heat: High and rising. Suspicion rests on the public voting record linking you to the dead wolf, with the investigator or other claimants naming you. Forward exposure: Any statement about the shared vote commits you to a stated reason that the room can check against the permanent public voting record. Directly attacking a confirmed result is irreversible, while a redirect toward a third suspect can be softened or dropped later. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed investigator or other claimed Town roles whose results are backed by the death record, and quiet unclaimed players with little evidence against them. The quiet players are the only workable redirect targets. The vote linkage is hard evidence, while suspicion of the quiet players rests on behavior. Public vs private: Privately you are the surviving wolf and know your partner's true role and the concealed kill. Publicly the partner is a revealed wolf and you are the only voter linked to them, so the room reads you as the likely second wolf.

action: If a Town player's night result clears you, such as a sigil that did not strike or a check that read Not suspicious, bring it up as your defense. Use only what the rules show: the sigil not triggering means only that you did not attack on that night, and it does not clear you of being a wolf. Pair it with a concrete alternative suspect so Town players with a stake in that result, such as the sigilist, have a reason to move their votes.
situation: Your wolf partner has been revealed and killed. You are pressured over a lone vote against a dead Town player, while a Town player's result (a non-triggering sigil) is available as a defense. Information landscape: Moderate: public voting records and a privately held Town result that can be used to clear you, but no hard role confirmations on the quiet alternative suspect. Stakes: Each vote now decides whether the last wolf survives. Moving even a couple of swing voters off you keeps the wolf team alive into the final few players. Consensus: The village is split. Some players press you over the vote record, while players holding a clearing result and neutral voters are open to another suspect. My position: holding out Heat: High. Players cite your isolated vote against a now-dead player as the basis for suspicion. Forward exposure: Citing a Town player's result ties you to a non-attacking story that you cannot take back, and later tracking evidence could break it. The alternative-suspect push can be adjusted as new information arrives.
