Target landscape: One or two suspects chosen from behavior, such as a lone vote against a claimed trailseer or being caught visiting someone. None is confirmed. Their seat positions relative to the previous kill carrier are known, or can be worked out if the wolves' identities are guessed.

action: Aim the sigil at a player whose evidence points to attacking, such as one a tracker caught visiting another player, or one who broke ranks to vote against a claimed town investigator. Do not pick a player merely because they visited a victim's door. Protective roles, the healer especially, also visit, and a visit by a non-attacker leaves the sigil with no effect.
situation: After a night attack or a save, you must choose which visitor or suspect to sigil. Visitors include both a likely attacker and a likely protector. Information landscape: Information-rich but ambiguous. Visit lists and claims exist, but they cannot separate an attacker from a protector. Stakes: Misreading a protector as an attacker wastes the final sigil, and Town loses its reactive deterrent while the wolves and the lone killer are still alive. Forward exposure: The sigil is spent as soon as it is placed, and a no-effect result leaves it unclear whether your target was innocent or just did not attack. You also lose any night ability for the rest of the game. Target landscape: Several players who visited a door or voted oddly. One has a tracker-linked or voting-anomaly signal tied to aggression. Another is a likely protector, such as a claimed healer or a visitor to a saved player. Roles are mostly unverified.

action: With your last sigil and your role exposed or under suspicion, place it on the player you most suspect of attacking tonight instead of holding it. If one wolf is left, that wolf always carries the kill, so it is the best target. If two or more wolves are left, pick the one whose seat turn to carry is next. A sigil you never place is lost if you are voted out, and a miss still costs nothing beyond the charge.
situation: Midgame with one sigil left. Your sigilist identity is exposed or a likely vote target, and the wolves and a lone killer are still hunting. Holding the charge risks a day-vote elimination that wastes it. Information landscape: Info-starved. There is one confirmed wolf role from an elimination, a few unverified claims, and a thin vote record. No hard evidence says who will attack tonight. Stakes: Town still has room to lose players, but each night kill costs a power role. A sigil strike on a carrier would remove a wolf or killer without a vote. An unused charge expires with you and gives town nothing. Forward exposure: Placing the sigil is a visit but stays secret unless the target attacks, so it commits you to nothing in public. A strike would be announced as a sigil death. A miss can be disclosed or kept hidden later, and either way the sigil is spent for good. Target landscape: Remaining wolf teammates of a confirmed-dead wolf, suspected killers, and quiet unclaimed players. Evidence is thin and mostly behavioral: an outlier vote, a soft-cleared player, or who has not yet carried. Public claims from other town roles are unverified.

action: When named as a quiet unknown in a small endgame, answer right away and don't stay silent. Cite confirmed facts (a dead Investigator's will, spent claims, public vote records) to show where you stand, then steer the room to the other unconfirmed player's contradictions or voting history. Frame the case on verified information, not on a rival's confusion over rules, so the vote lands on the actual wolf.
situation: Four players are left after the lone killer and several roles have died. The town must pick the last wolf among unconfirmed players, and the speculator is under pressure for staying quiet and revealing nothing. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, a posthumous investigator will, spent claims and a complete public voting history. A vote misfire here is costly. Stakes: At four alive with a wolf still in play, one wrong elimination lets the wolves reach parity and win, which would defeat a Town pick. Each vote decides the game. Consensus: The room is split between the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players. Cleared town players are still choosing, and the discussion is concrete and focused on the endgame. My position: Driving: actively shaping which unconfirmed player the room pursues. Heat: High: two or more players have named the speculator as a quiet, unclaimed unknown who stayed under the radar. Target landscape: A small endgame in which the speculator and one or two other unconfirmed players are the remaining suspects. Dead roles are confirmed. Cases rest on wills, vote history and claim consistency, and the speculator has claimed nothing.

action: When a claimed role demands your role while two others trade accusations over conflicting logs, don't build the case on a rule-confusion or a thin data gap. Test the contradiction against the rules, for example whether a watch counts as a visit and who could have seen what. Back the elimination only if the mechanics actually prove a lie, and otherwise hold your vote for the player whose claim can't be explained.
situation: With four players alive and one wolf left, a claimed vigilante demands the speculator's role while the claimed sentinel and claimed trailseer accuse each other over contradictory logs. Information landscape: Information-rich in confirmed dead roles, but the key conflict is between unverified claims, and a rules-confusion slip is being treated as proof. Stakes: At four alive with one wolf left, a wrong elimination likely hands the wolves the win. Pushing a mis-vote also exposes the speculator to a night shot. Consensus: The room leans toward whoever the credible shooter points at. It is tied up in the conflicting tracking logs and is pressuring the speculator for transparency. My position: Driving: pushing the accusation of one of the conflicting claimants to deflect heat. Heat: High: a credible claimed role singled the speculator out as a suspect for withholding its role all game. Target landscape: Two claimed roles, for example a sentinel and a trailseer, with logs that conflict, plus the speculator, who is being pressed for a role. The vigilante's shot gives it credibility, while the sentinel's and trailseer's results are unverified claims.

action: When the room is working from public records (votes, confirmed roles) and someone misstates a fact, correct it plainly by citing the exact record, and keep your own suspicion reads low-profile. Don't float speculative doubts about a claimed role's credibility without hard evidence, since they leave a lasting rift that evil players can exploit later against you.
situation: Mid-game day discussion after night deaths (confirmed and concealed bodies); the room debates the previous day's voting record and a claimed investigator's result, and someone misremembers the record or the room begins to doubt a claim. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, public voting records and at least one claimed investigator check, though the claims are unverified. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions still alive; one mis-elimination can hand tempo to the wolves or the lone killer. The speculator has not yet picked, or is about to pick, and needs Town to keep eliminating evil players. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around the public Day 2 voting record and the claimed investigator's check, and is largely converging on a suspect. My position: With the majority; not driving any accusation, supporting record accuracy rather than a specific target. Heat: None to low; the speculator is seen as a neutral, helpful contributor, with no accusations against it until it voices contrarian doubts. Target landscape: Several candidates sorted by public record: confirmed dead roles, a claimed investigator whose check is unverified, a quiet player, and an unconfirmed player with a suspicious vote. Basis is a mix of hard voting records and behavioral reads.

action: While no heat is on you and the room is split over competing claims, anchor your comments on facts the Game Master announced (a save, a death, a revealed role) and on what the rules allow. Stay neutral on the claim dispute, and use the quiet to see which side is gaining ground, since a Speculator that dies before picking loses.
situation: The morning after a night attack, with a save or a roleblock reported, a claim conflict erupts between rival investigator or healer claimants, or an unprompted visit report triggers a push on the reporter. The speculator is unpressured and has not yet picked a side. Information landscape: Information-rich: an announced save or death, claimed night results, and rival claims whose contradictions can be tested against announced facts. Stakes: Mid-game with several players alive. No single vote flips the game yet, so the speculator should stay alive and gather evidence before committing its pick. Consensus: The village is converging on resolving the claim conflict, with attention on the contested claimants and not on quiet players. My position: With the majority, in a grounding, non-leading role. Heat: None. No one has voiced suspicion of the speculator, and the room's attention is on the claim conflict. Target landscape: Competing role claims (two investigators or two healers) and an unverified door-traffic or night-result report. Public announcements are the only verified anchor, and the rest is claim versus claim.

action: At four alive with one wolf left and a Town pick, cast your vote on the player whose claim is contradicted by hard, announced evidence (wills, confirmed kills, cleared roles), not on one side of a he-said-she-said about how an ability works. If the only basis is a disputed claim about a mechanic, check it against the rules text first, because a wrong lynch leaves Town one body from parity and loses your pick.
situation: Endgame day vote at four alive with one wolf remaining after the lone killer is dead; two claimed Town roles contradict each other and the group must pick who is lying. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed deaths, public wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill exist, but the decisive dispute is two unverified night claims. Stakes: One wrong elimination leaves three players with the wolf one kill from parity, so the vote decides whether Town wins or the wolves win and the Town pick loses. Consensus: The room leans toward eliminating one claimed player based on a claim contradiction, with the Vigilante driving it. My position: With the majority, joining the Vigilante and Trailseer vote. Heat: High: the Vigilante accuses the Speculator of concealing their role and dodging deduction, though the room's immediate target is the Sentinel. Target landscape: Four survivors: a claimed Vigilante, a claimed Sentinel and a claimed Trailseer with contradictory night-action claims, plus the unclaimed Speculator. Public evidence is eliminated players' wills and a confirmed Vigilante kill. Evidence against the Sentinel is only a disputed claim about whether watching is a visit, while the rules say watching is a visit.

action: When four are alive, one wolf remains, and the Speculator has picked Town, join the cleared Town players in eliminating the one unverified suspect rather than the other. Ignore the suspect's counter-accusation of you when it rests only on a quiet record, because eliminating the last wolf ends the game with a Town win and your pick wins.
situation: Final-wolf vote at four alive: the village must eliminate the last wolf now or face parity at night, and the Speculator is one of the two unverified players. Information landscape: Information-rich: the dead Investigator's will clears one player, the Sigilist's abilities are logged and spent, and the lone killer is confirmed dead. Stakes: Eliminating the last wolf wins immediately for Town and for a Town pick, while a miss leaves three alive with parity at night. Consensus: Two confirmed Town players treat the vote as a choice between the two unverified players and are open to a clear case. My position: With the majority, voting alongside the cleared players. Heat: Exposed: the remaining suspect openly pushes to eliminate the agent based on a quiet record, and the confirmed Town players see it as a binary choice. Target landscape: Two unverified players, the Speculator and one suspect who survived earlier scrutiny, among four alive. The other two are cleared or confirmed Town, by a dead Investigator's will and spent, logged abilities. The suspect's push on the Speculator is behavioral, while the confirmed Town players are the deciding votes.

action: At four alive with a Town pick and evil one step from parity, treat the vote as match point: before voting, state your read and the evidence, and vote with the largest bloc that excludes the most likely evil player, or push for a tie if no bloc is safe. If the room is converging on you and you cannot flip it, shift the vote toward the strongest remaining evil candidate rather than casting a lone vote that changes nothing.
situation: Late game, four alive, one evil faction a single elimination from winning. The speculator's own vote is isolated against a forming wagon, and either its elimination or a wasted vote lets evil reach parity. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed roles of the dead, public voting histories, and some investigator or trailseer claims, but nothing that proves who is evil. Stakes: One vote decides whether Town keeps enough living bodies to stay ahead; an isolated vote or the speculator's own death hands evil parity the next night, and the speculator's Town pick fails with it. Consensus: The room is nearly unanimous or splitting two ways around a wagon, built on past votes and dead players' records rather than night results. My position: Holding out with an isolated vote against the wagon. Heat: Moderate to severe: accused by the room, or by a quiet suspect, as deflecting, or tied to a dead player's earlier vote. Target landscape: Three or four living players at match point: a surviving evil player (wolf or serial killer) identified only through past voting alignment, the claimed or reliable Town players, and the speculator itself as a counter-target. Evidence is voting records and confirmed deaths, not hard role proof.

action: When you have already picked Town and the day vote is split among several candidates, cast your vote sincerely on the unconfirmed player whose behavior or claims look most evil. Prefer the candidate whose claims conflict with other players' reports over a claimed Town power role. Your vote can swing a split or tie, so use it to stop a Town-aligned elimination and to remove the likeliest killer, which keeps Town the winning side you picked.
situation: The speculator has already picked a side (Town) and sits in a split or deadlocked day vote where its single vote can decide a tie or prevent a bad elimination of a claimed Town role. Both wolves and a lone killer may still be alive. Information landscape: Moderate and muddled: night kills, a hidden role, conflicting role claims and night-result claims, but no confirmed wolf or killer. Mostly unverified claims plus voting records. Stakes: With about six players alive and two killing factions active, one vote can decide an elimination or block a Town loss. A mistaken Town elimination moves evil toward parity and weakens the Town side the speculator picked. Consensus: The village is scattered or split into near-equal camps with no single dominant target; the push is based on muddled claims and behavioral reads. My position: with majority Heat: Low to none; nobody has directed accusations at the speculator, and its speech has been neutral. Target landscape: Several candidates split the room: claimed Town power roles (healer, trailseer, sigilist, vigilante) versus an unconfirmed quiet or counter-accusing player. The evidence is partly claims and conflicting timelines, partly behavior and past votes, with no confirmed wolf.

action: On nights 1-2, while no evil role has been confirmed eliminated and no claim has been tested, keep the one-time pick unspent. Reassess each night, and commit as soon as board evidence clearly favors one side or you suspect you are likely to be killed. Dying unpicked is a loss, but an uninformed early lock-in has no advantage, and the pick cannot be changed once made.
situation: Early game, night 1 or 2, with a discussion-only day 1 or an abstained day 2. At most one or two night deaths so far, and neither wolves nor the lone killer have been exposed. The speculator is still unpicked and has not been targeted. Information landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed evil eliminations, only unverified claims and concealed or ambiguous bodies, and no momentum signal for any faction. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is no immediate pressure to lock in. The only cost of waiting is the risk of dying unpicked, which is low on night 1 and rises as killers act. Holding costs little and keeps the option open for an informed pick later. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self, or keep holding. All ten players are alive with no confirmed roles and no tested claims. Any pick would be a pure guess on behavior, not evidence.

action: Once the day vote has system-confirmed an evil elimination and the surviving power-role claims are validated, make the pick on that night instead of waiting longer. Choose Town only if the lone killer is confirmed gone or Town clearly outnumbers a single remaining wolf; if killers are still active with an uncertain Town lead, keep holding until one side is clearly ahead, unless you are likely to be killed that night.
situation: Night 3 after Town's day vote eliminated a confirmed wolf or lone killer, with healer saves publicly verified. Town holds a large majority, but some killers remain. Past observations show the Town pick won when Town stayed disciplined and lost when Town later mis-eliminated its own power roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: system-confirmed evil role reveals, a validated investigator claim, and announced healer saves. The remaining unknown is whether a wolf or killer is still hidden and how well Town will play. Stakes: Town leads, but a few mis-votes or kills could still flip the game, so the pick is only as good as Town's later play. Picking now removes the risk of dying unpicked, but it ties your win to Town's survival and avoiding errors. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self. After a confirmed evil elimination Town looks dominant, with validated investigator or healer claims and a numerical majority. Evil still has a wolf and possibly an unknown lone killer, and Town's later errors can still erase that lead.

action: When your follow result places a living player at a victim's door, or contradicts a suspect's account, reveal the Trailseer role and state the result plainly. Demand the suspect explain the visit, and answer mechanical objections by citing only the stated rules while treating your result as your own claim. Push the room to a vote on that suspect.
situation: After a night death (often with a concealed role), the Trailseer holds a follow result tying a player to the victim. The town doubts whether the result is real or possible. Information landscape: Information-rich: several days of claims, a dead player with a concealed role, and a direct follow result linking a living player to the scene. Stakes: Town is still ahead but cannot afford a wasted vote. Removing a wolf early strips the pack of abilities and moves the wolves further from parity. Consensus: The room is hesitant and split. Players are unsure what evidence is usable, and no one has a hard lead besides yours. My position: Driving the accusation with the only concrete evidence available. Heat: Moderate to high once you claim: the accused and a few skeptics call the claim fabricated or mechanically impossible. Forward exposure: Revealing the role and result commits you to a direct 1-for-1 conflict with the suspect and makes you a likely target for night kills or blocks. It cannot be undone, but it gives the town a hard lead. Target landscape: A quiet or vocal suspect tied to the murder scene by your follow result, versus counter-accusations against you. The basis is a private movement log, not behavior alone. Public vs private: You privately hold a concrete follow trail that points at one player, while the room is confused about what can be tracked or whether any visit can be traced after a hidden-role death.

action: When you were roleblocked or when claims collide, state your own result or block and point the room at the rule-level contradiction. Examples are two Investigator claimants when only one Investigator exists, or a player citing visitor information after the Sentinel is dead. Question the claimant directly about their source so attention stays on the conflict instead of side topics.
situation: Two players make clashing claims, or one makes an impossible knowledge claim. A healer save or a dead role is on record, and the Trailseer has private confirmation of evil disruption. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced saves and deaths, voting records, and claims that can be checked against the rules. Stakes: A single vote on the right claimant can remove a wolf or the lone killer. Letting a false claimant survive would hand evil a deflection. Consensus: The room is open and leaning toward whoever resolves the contradiction. There is a cooperative core of confirmed or credible town claims. My position: Driving the interrogation alongside credible town claimants. Heat: None to low: the town sees you as a cooperative, informational voice. Forward exposure: Disclosing a roleblock reveals that you hold an active night action and makes you a possible target for further blocks or kills. The reveal is reversible and low-cost because it only backs claims that already exist. Target landscape: Players whose claims clash with the rules or with announced facts, such as a counter-claimant or a player claiming information from a dead role, versus plausible but unproven players. The basis is claim logic, not just behavior. Public vs private: You privately know someone is actively disrupting night actions, and that confirms the evil activity the room is only guessing at. Publicly there are conflicting claims or an unexplained player claim.

action: When the board is down to 3-4 players, share your night result and use it to name one remaining player as your target. Say which public claim your result contradicts, or which player it clears, and ask the swing voter to confirm anything they can. Do not call the other players' debate bickering or stay neutral, because that leaves the wolf or killer free to redirect the vote.
situation: Late-game endgame at 3-4 alive with one wolf or lone killer left. The trailseer holds a private visit result that bears on a rival's claim, and a wrong vote means a parity loss at the next night kill. Information landscape: Information-rich: night deaths and roles are revealed, claims are on the table, and voting logs and earlier tracking and sigil histories are known. Only the final identification is missing. Stakes: One wrong elimination leaves a single night kill from parity or an evil win, so this vote is decisive. Town can only win by identifying the last evil player now, and the trailseer's result is the key evidence. Consensus: The village is split and open to persuasion. Debate is split between voting-record arguments and claims, and nobody has hard proof, so the swing voter's choice decides it. My position: Driving the accusation. You are the one who has to frame the evidence, not holding out between sides. Heat: Moderate to high. A rival claimant may be accusing you of fabricating tracking reports or pushing for your elimination, based on passive results. Forward exposure: Sharing the result and naming a target commits you to a win-or-lose confrontation that can't be walked back. It puts your tracking claim on the line for the swing voter to check. Staying vague keeps you flexible but gives up control of the vote. Target landscape: A binary or three-way choice among the few survivors, such as a claimed sentinel against the trailseer with a claimed sigilist as swing voter. Evidence is thin: the trailseer's visit results, past voting records, and claims from dead players. The best target is the one whose claim your result contradicts. Public vs private: You privately know a specific visit result, such as a claimed role making zero visits on the key night. It either contradicts or bypasses the public accusation, and the room is still debating on past votes or other players' claims.

action: When your night tracking places a dead or suspected player's final visit on a living player and the room has no stronger lead, vote that visited player rather than splitting onto a different suspect. If the visit is your only hard evidence, state it plainly so others can converge, because a split vote leaves a surviving wolf alive and able to kill you at night.
situation: Few players remain after an information role's death. You reported tracking the investigator to a living suspect, yet the vote splits between that suspect and a claimed protective role, and a tie would eliminate no one. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead investigator, a confirmed save, and your own tracked visit give concrete leads, though they are not verified by the Game Master. Stakes: With seven alive and a wolf still active, every day vote is a chance to remove a wolf. A tied vote wastes it and gives the wolf another night to kill, possibly you. Consensus: The village is split and distracted by argument over how simultaneous night actions resolve, with no common read on whom to eliminate. My position: holding out Heat: Moderate: a surviving wolf is publicly attacking your credibility and your grasp of how visits work, so you are already a likely night target. Forward exposure: Voting is public and permanent. Voting your own tracked lead commits you to a consistent story and shows the room your result is sincere, while voting against it contradicts your own report and cannot be taken back. Target landscape: Two main candidates: the living player your tracking tied to the dead investigator's last visit, which is private evidence of a visit but not proof of role, and a claimed healer under behavioral suspicion for a disputed roleblock claim. The tracked visit is the stronger basis. Public vs private: You privately know whom the dead investigator last visited, while public talk is distracted by side disputes such as simultaneous-action mechanics and suspicion of a claimed protective role.

action: When the wolves are gone but a killer remains, the investigator's checks are spent, and your tracking shows only stationary results, do not abstain by default. Vote for the candidate with the most behavioral basis, such as deflecting attention onto others, and say why. An abstain hands control to a fragmented room that may eliminate a town role.
situation: Both wolves are eliminated and the investigator is out of checks, so the village scatters accusations across several unconfirmed players while a lone killer remains. Information landscape: Information-starved: the checks are spent, the healer's target is public, and your own tracking gave only stationary results. Stakes: With few players left and a lone killer alive, each mistaken elimination of a town role brings the killer closer to winning. Leaving the vote to a scattered room risks that outcome. Consensus: Discussion is fractured into competing accusations with no majority, because no checks or confirmed roles remain to anchor a read. My position: holding out Heat: Low: you earlier backed the investigator's mechanics and are treated as a trusted town asset. Forward exposure: An abstain is low-risk and keeps your credibility, but it concedes the outcome to scattered votes. A committed vote exposes your reasoning, though it can be explained and revised on later days. Target landscape: A split field of unconfirmed players: a quiet one, one deflecting attention onto others, and a reserved one with no claimed role. None has hard evidence against them, so the choice rests on behavior. Public vs private: Your private tracking showed a stationary result for the claimed investigator, which confirms the public read but gives no lead on the remaining killer.

action: When few players remain and your private follow results either put a target at the scene of a night kill or clear a rival suspect (they visited no one), vote to eliminate the target your tracking implicates. Do this even if the target counter-accuses you, because your own follow record outweighs their claims. If the follow result clears both candidates, fall back on role-pool elimination and claim consistency.
situation: Endgame day vote with 3-4 players alive. Most evil and most town info roles are dead, and the remaining accused claims a town role and counter-accuses the trailseer. The trailseer's private follow trace either places the accused at a night kill or shows a rival suspect staying home. Information landscape: Information-rich. Public death records have eliminated most roles from the pool, and the trailseer holds a concrete private follow result, either a visit to the murder victim or no visits, that checks against the claims. Stakes: The vote is decisive. With so few players alive, the next elimination either ends the game in Town's favor by removing the last hostile player or moves the evil side to parity. The trailseer's vote may be the kingmaker. Consensus: The few survivors are split or leaning in different directions. The trailseer's follow evidence is the main basis for forming a decisive majority, since the dead roles narrow the pool. My position: driving Heat: Moderate pressure from the accused hostile player, who reframes the trailseer's follow results as suspicious or calls them fabricated. The rest of the room is not hostile to the trailseer. Forward exposure: The final vote is public, permanent and irreversible. A correct vote eliminates the last hostile player and ends the game; a wrong one risks handing parity to the evil side. Voting also commits the trailseer to the follow evidence, which the accused will attack. Target landscape: Two or three candidates remain. One is the accused, who claims a town role such as sentinel or vigilante and counter-attacks the trailseer. The other is a claimed role whose night record matches the trailseer's private follow. The choice rests on private visit evidence plus role-pool elimination from public death records, not on tone. Public vs private: Privately followed a suspect and saw either a visit to that night's murder victim or no visits at all. This confirms the public case against the accused and contradicts the accused's counter-accusation against the trailseer.

action: On day 2, when you have publicly reported a tracking result, the room favors abstaining, and no player has been confirmed evil, vote to abstain with the majority rather than pushing a solo elimination on the player you followed. If that player's story later contradicts your report or the rules, keep your report as the evidence and wait for the next night's tracking result before committing a vote.
situation: After day 1 the trailseer reported whom a player visited. On day 2 the followed player disputes or deflects the report and casts a retaliatory vote on the trailseer, while the rest of the village leans toward abstaining. Information landscape: Mostly claims: a tracking report, perhaps a sentinel watch or sigil claim, and one or two night deaths with roles announced or hidden. There are no verified links to guilt. Stakes: The board is mid-game with several evil factions still alive. A wrong elimination costs Town more than a skipped day, so a no-kill day is cheap while evidence is thin. Consensus: The village is strongly aligned on waiting and abstaining, because night results are inconclusive and nobody has hard evidence. The consensus rests on caution, not on a shared suspect. My position: with majority Heat: Low from the room overall. The tracked player casts a retaliatory vote or questions your report, which is isolated, not a village-wide suspicion. Forward exposure: Abstaining with the majority commits you to nothing and is reversible on later days. A solo push on the tracked player would tie your claimed role to one unverified accusation and make you the visible driver. Target landscape: The only individual under scrutiny is the player you followed, who gave a contradictory or hollow account. They have no confirmed role and the case rests on behavior against your own report. No other candidate has evidence against them. Public vs private: You privately know whom the tracked player visited (or that they visited no one) and have shared it. The tracked player disputes or muddies it, but nothing is verified, so the public read stays unresolved.

action: When a death or a role flip leaves a specific suspect, or a specific pair of visitors, in dispute, follow that suspect, or the visitor whose role is least verified. Their visit shows whether they go to the night's victim or to a claimed role, and that is hard evidence for the next day's vote. If a follow comes back blocked, the block itself is evidence about that player.
situation: Mid-game after a night death or a confirmed wolf flip, the village is divided over a suspect or over which of two visitors is the real healer. The trailseer can follow one player to turn that dispute into a concrete visit record. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed flips, public claims, voting records and the visit reports of other roles give a clear suspect pool. The trailseer's own tracking can add a hard data point. Stakes: The board is mid-game with evil still alive. One reliable visit record can settle a lynch decision and remove a wolf, so tracking the most contested player pays off more than a random follow. Target landscape: A small set of contested players: someone who defended a flipped wolf, a visitor to an attacked player whose role is unverified, or a quiet player the village is eyeing. Candidates are chosen on behavior and public disputes. The claimed roles in the room are already partly vetted.

action: When the trailseer's own role is likely to draw an attack, follow the player the wolves most want dead, such as the confirmed investigator who just exposed a wolf. If the target dies, the trailseer still learns whom they visited that night. That information can point suspicion at the visited player.
situation: A wolf was just eliminated by the vote, and the confirmed town investigator is the obvious target for wolf retaliation that night. The trailseer wants to preserve that investigator's last action in case they are killed. Information landscape: Info-rich: a wolf has been caught, the investigator is validated, and earlier night visits and claims are on record. Visit data on the likely victim is more valuable than a blind follow. Stakes: Losing the investigator without recovering their last check would remove a key information source. Seeing the investigator's visit, and getting it reported, can lead directly to the last wolf. Target landscape: The confirmed or strongly vetted info role facing retaliation, versus claimed protectors who were already attacked or saved, versus quiet unread players. The vetted role is the likeliest night victim and a natural way to find their last target.

action: On Night 1, with no claims or votes yet, follow one quiet unvetted player and pick someone other than yourself who is not already pressing you. Expect the wolves to kill early information roles, so take the best available baseline visit. If you survive, the result gives a location or a lone-killer or wolf visit to build on.
situation: Night 1 after a no-vote Day 1: nobody has claimed a role, nobody has voted, and the trailseer has to choose a follow target blind. Wolves may kill the trailseer that night, which would leave the result undelivered. Information landscape: Info-starved: no claims, no flips, no voting record and no night results. Any pick is arbitrary. Stakes: Early in the game there is room to absorb a miss, but a trailseer killed on Night 1 delivers nothing. A follow that catches a visit can still anchor later reads, so a quick blind pick is acceptable. Target landscape: All nine other players are unvetted and unclaimed. There is no behavioral basis, so any quiet or low-profile player is as good as another, and the aim is to catch a visit to or from a night actor.

action: On the opening night with no claims or reads, follow one unread, low-profile player to get a concrete movement baseline. If the result names a door, keep it as a checkable link to cross-reference against other night results and later claims. If it shows no visits, treat that as weak information, because a wolf carrier whose victim was concealed leaves no trace, and the target may also be a passive role.
situation: Opening night after a discussion-only Day 1. The Trailseer must pick a first follow target blindly, while the wolves and a lone killer may also pick arbitrary opening kills, including the Trailseer. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no voting record, no night history, only baseline impressions from Day 1. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive and evil far from parity, so no single follow is decisive. The value is in collecting a first concrete visit link before wagons and claims form, and the Trailseer may be killed before reporting it. Target landscape: Nine unrevealed other players with no claims, votes or behavioral deviations; any pick is an exploratory behavioral guess, so choose an unread player who does not stand out.

action: Late in an info-rich game, follow the unverified claimant who is a live suspect and whose claimed role is not a night attacker (or who says they are holding shots). If they visit the night's victim, you have direct evidence against them, so bring that visit to the town as your result. If they visit no one, treat it only as consistent with holding an ability, not as a clearing, and next night follow another suspect.
situation: Late game after wolf kills or eliminations, with a killer still hidden among a few suspects. Town must find the remaining evil player and the Trailseer can follow only one suspect each night. One follow can produce a decisive visit trace, or a null result that tells little. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead wolves and roles are confirmed, claims are made, and voting records are on the table. Only a small set of unverified claimants is left. A follow result gives the Trailseer hard private evidence. Stakes: Few players remain, so one wrong vote or one missed night can let evil reach parity or win. The Trailseer's follow is likely the best source of hard evidence on the board, and a follow on the wrong suspect wastes a night that cannot be spared. Target landscape: A few unverified suspects: claimed power-role holders (sigilist, vigilante) who say they are holding abilities, plus a quiet player. Their claims are unconfirmed, so the decision rests on behavior and vote alignment, not hard evidence. Choose the one whose claim is most consistent with night attacks.

action: When your only lead is a behavioral slip or an abstention, put it to the suspect as a specific, checkable question and state your confidence as partial. Do not assert their guilt or push the room toward a vote on it. If their answer fits the rules and the other claims, move to the next candidate; if it still contradicts them, keep pressing without staking your credibility on one verdict.
situation: After an early death or elimination, the village scrutinizes one player who made an inconsistent statement or abstained. I, a hidden vigilante with bullets left, am the one driving the accusation on behavior alone. Information landscape: Thin and behavioral: a few deaths and claims, conflicting explanations, and no verified result pointing at the target. The accusation rests on talk, not mechanics. Stakes: Both evil factions are likely still alive and town cannot afford a wasted day-vote. A wrongly eliminated town or neutral player shrinks town toward parity without removing a threat, so the accusation needs more care than its low heat suggests. Consensus: The room is loosely aligned and quick to follow a confident accuser. It has no hard evidence, so it can pile onto one target within a round. My position: driving Heat: Low. The village treats me as a constructive voice and nobody suspects me. Forward exposure: Aggressive accusation commits my credibility to one target, and a unanimous vote cannot be undone. Framed as a question, it stays reversible, and I stay unrevealed as vigilante and out of wolf night attention. Target landscape: A claimed role with a shaky or inconsistent explanation, or an abstainer, versus quiet unchecked players. No hard investigative clears separate them, so the basis is behavior, not evidence. Public vs private: I hold bullets and no private evidence on the target. My suspicion rests only on a public stumble or an abstention, so I know no more than the room does.

action: While heat is low, keep the vigilante role hidden and use discussion to widen the pool. Ask the investigator, sentinel and other claimants to say which players their results cover, and have the room rank the unchecked players. This keeps your bullets as a private option and stops a single behavioral read from becoming the consensus.
situation: One evil threat has just been eliminated and the village hunts the next target among the unchecked. I am a quiet vigilante with bullets left and can shape how the room searches. Information landscape: Fairly informative: confirmed roles, cleared players and a visibly active protector. Only the unchecked pool is unresolved, and it is judged by behavior. Stakes: Town still has its protective and investigative roles, so there is room to be careful. Losing them to a rushed vote would cost more than waiting one more round of discussion. Consensus: The village is aligned on trusting confirmed results and looking for targets among the uncleared pool. It has no settled suspect yet. My position: with majority Heat: Low to none. Town attention is on the sentinel's and investigator's information, and nobody is looking at me. Forward exposure: Steering discussion toward checked versus unchecked players reveals nothing about my role and commits me to no single target. I can still shoot later or join whichever read hardens. Target landscape: Unchecked players with no investigative clears, ranked by behavior and by what the claimed roles' results cover. No target is confirmed. Public vs private: Privately I hold shots, but town attention is on confirmed information from other roles. Staying quiet about my role costs nothing now.

action: When claimed town roles are demanding that unclaimed players account for themselves, or you are named in a narrow suspect pool, claim vigilante in discussion before the vote and state your bullet count. If you still have bullets, offer to shoot a named suspect that night, so the room has a reason to keep you alive; a vigilante who stays silent and is voted out wastes every bullet and gives a lone killer a corpse to use.
situation: Late-game role-call: wolves are mostly or entirely dead, claimed town roles have cleared themselves, and the remaining unclaimed players are pressed to reveal roles or be voted out. I am a silent vigilante inside that pool. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles are revealed, claimed roles are backed by night results, and the suspect pool is narrowed to a few players. Only the unclaimed players remain unexplained. Stakes: With few players alive, one wrongful vote on me can hand a surviving killer parity or free body access. Losing a vigilante with bullets forfeits town's remaining way to kill an unseen threat. Consensus: The village is aligned around claimed, partly verified town roles and is converging on the unclaimed players. The basis is elimination by role-count, not hard evidence against any one player. My position: holding_out Heat: High and rising: claimed town roles are demanding role declarations from unclaimed players, or have named me as one of the last suspects. I have no defense on record. Forward exposure: Claiming reveals the vigilante role and its remaining firepower, and wolves or a lone killer can target me at night. The claim is not reversible, but staying silent risks being voted out with every bullet unspent. Day 1 has no vote, so a claim there carries less immediate risk than one made right before a vote. Target landscape: A tiny unclaimed pool (me, a hidden killer or wolf, and a quiet neutral or unverified player) facing a claimed town bloc. The reads rest on behavior and silence, since the claimed roles are confirmed only by night results. Public vs private: I privately know I am the genuine town vigilante with unspent bullets, but the room reads my silence as evasion and treats me as the likely hidden lone killer or wolf.

action: When a claimed investigator or sigilist is already the focus and the room is information-rich, back the claim with sincere, verifiable reasoning (a public result about you, or the logic of a confirmed save), and stay with the majority. Do not mention the vigilante role or bullet count; keep your shots for ambiguous threats later.
situation: A claimed power role (investigator or sigilist) has produced a result that implicates an aggressive player or mentions me. Their credibility is being contested by a counter-claim or by an accusation of fabrication. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced healer saves, attacks the claimant survived, reported results and visits, and prior wolf eliminations give the room checkable facts. Stakes: The board is mid-game with a few non-town players left. Consolidating a vote on a likely wolf is valuable, while losing the vigilante's shots to a night kill or roleblock would cost much more than speaking up gains. Consensus: The village is converging on one lead, backed by announced night facts such as a healer save or a dual attack survived, and there is little dissent. My position: with_majority Heat: Zero or minimal. A claimed investigator or sigilist has cleared me, or my status is simply not under question, and nobody is accusing me. Forward exposure: Corroborating a result about myself or reasoning from confirmed night reports reveals nothing about my role or shots. A vigilante claim would draw wolf kills and roleblocks and could not be taken back. Target landscape: The main candidates are the player accused by a claimed investigator, or a counter-claimant contradicting a claimed investigator or sigilist. They are weighed by announced saves, reported visits and checks against the accused's defensive claims of fabrication. Public vs private: Privately I hold the vigilante's shots and my role is unknown. Publicly I am a low-heat villager whose cleared or consistent status matches what a claimed power role reported about me.

action: When your night shot produced a result the Game Master's morning report or your private feedback can corroborate (a death announced as a vigilante shot, or an immune-target notice), claim vigilante at dawn and state exactly what you shot and what happened. If the shot hit a night-immune target, name that player as the Serial Killer and lead the vote on them; if it killed a wolf, say how many threats remain and put forward the next test.
situation: After a night shot that produced a verifiable result, either a vigilante kill announced by the Game Master or a private immune-target notice, the vigilante has one bullet left and the town needs direction against the remaining killers. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced deaths, dead Town wills, healer save history, and the vigilante's own private shot feedback give mechanic-backed evidence. Stakes: With few players alive, a single vote or night kill decides the game. Leading the correct elimination now, or keeping the last bullet for the lone killer, decides whether town survives. Consensus: The village is receptive and rallies around claims backed by announced facts, and it is looking for someone to organize the next step. My position: driving the discussion and the vote Heat: Low to zero from the town majority, because the claim matches the Game Master's announcement or a checkable mechanic. An accused player may call it a fabrication, but that has little traction. Forward exposure: Hard-claiming vigilante with a bullet left gives up role secrecy and makes me a likely night-kill target, and the claim cannot be taken back. In exchange it earns concrete credibility and lets me steer the room. Target landscape: Remaining players are an unverified pool: a claimed healer, quiet players, spent roles, a neutral, and the player my shot exposed as immune or the one I killed. Public evidence (the death announcement, wills, healer saves) outweighs behavior reads. Public vs private: I privately know exactly whom I shot and what the result was, and the public record (the morning announcement, or the lack of one) lines up with that, so my claim can be checked against it.

action: With four alive, a wolf still in play and one or more bullets held, keep the vigilante role and bullets unannounced. Argue the vote only from confirmed facts, such as announced roles and read-out wills, and use your cleared standing to narrow the field to the unverified players. Announcing held bullets tells the surviving wolf exactly whom to kill that night, and a claim cannot be taken back.
situation: Endgame at four alive with one hidden evil player left, after announced deaths or wills have cleared me. The discussion decides the final vote, and my hidden bullet is my edge. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced roles and read-out wills, vote records, and eliminated threats give solid anchors. The remaining uncertainty is only among the few unverified players. Stakes: At four alive, a single mis-vote or night kill can hand the wolves parity and the win. Hiding the vigilante keeps the night kill from landing on me, and I keep a reserve shot. Consensus: The living players accept the confirmed facts and are turning scrutiny on each other rather than on me. They have no settled target yet. My position: driving Heat: Little or none, because system-confirmed information clears me and the room treats me as trusted town. Forward exposure: Claiming vigilante would reveal a live bullet and make me the wolf's priority night kill. Staying quiet costs nothing and the claim stays available later, while a claim cannot be undone. Target landscape: Two or three unverified players, none with a confirmed role, separated by voting records and behavior rather than hard evidence. I am already treated as cleared. Public vs private: Publicly I read as cleared town through an announced role or will, and privately I hold an unfired vigilante bullet the last wolf does not know about. Nothing in the room contradicts my private knowledge.

action: Before you accuse a claimed role of lying, check the accusation against the game rules. Accuse only if the contradiction is a real rules violation. If it is just confusion over wording, such as whether a watch counts as a visit, treat the player as possibly confused town and push the silent unclaimed player instead. A wrong accusation at four alive removes a town role and gives the wolf the win.
situation: Four alive with one wolf left. Two claimed information roles dispute whether a watch counts as a visit, and I have to decide whom to push as the wolf. Information landscape: Information-rich on paper (read-out wills, claimed results) but with irreconcilable living claims. A rules disagreement is being read as a lie. Stakes: Four alive with one wolf means one wrong elimination, plus the wolf's night kill, ends the game. There is no margin for a mis-vote. Consensus: The village is split between two conflicting claims and is willing to follow a confident accuser. Others tend to pile onto whichever read is argued most forcefully. My position: driving Heat: Moderate to high, since I am questioned and accused by the other claimed role and the unclaimed player before the vote. Forward exposure: Claiming vigilante and leading a vote on a rules-semantics argument commits my credibility and puts a live bullet in the wolf's sights. If the accusation is wrong the town cannot recover, because the vote is public and final. Target landscape: A claimed trailseer, a claimed sentinel, and an unclaimed silent player. The evidence is conflicting claims and one disputed rules point, with little behavioral proof against anyone. Public vs private: Privately I know I am the real vigilante with a bullet left, but I have no hidden knowledge about who the last wolf is. Publicly, two investigative claims conflict, and I could mistake a rules misunderstanding for wolf deception.

action: If the room is down to a few players and a revealed vigilante claim cannot be avoided, claim openly and press the unclaimed players to state their roles before the vote. Push the vote toward the most evidently evil player. Understand that revealing held bullets makes you the wolf's night target, so use the claim only when the day's elimination would decide the game.
situation: Four alive with a wolf and the necromancer both still alive. The day's vote has to eliminate an evil player or the game is lost. Information landscape: Information-rich: several dead town roles and a dead illusionist are confirmed, a claimed sentinel is spent, and two players remain unclaimed. Stakes: The vote must land on an evil player now, or evil reaches parity. A claim that wins the vote can still lose the night, so weigh both. Consensus: The room is fluid and looking for direction, and it follows a clear lead when claims are limited and pressure is applied. My position: driving Heat: Moderate, from an unclaimed player pointing at my late claim. Forward exposure: Claiming and revealing held bullets cannot be reversed, and it tells the surviving wolf whom to block or kill that night. It buys day leverage at the cost of night safety. Target landscape: Two unclaimed players under pressure to claim, versus a claimed role whose uses are exhausted. The case rests on claim status and behavior under pressure. Public vs private: Privately I hold full ammunition and I tell the room openly. There is no gap between my private knowledge and what the public will see.

action: When the room is converging on you and you still hold bullets, put your vote on the strongest competing suspect, the one already drawing votes, to force a tie or split the ballot. Do not cast a lone vote on a third candidate, because a tie means no elimination and keeps your bullets alive for the night.
situation: Late day vote with the evil pool narrowed to a few unverified players. Suspicion has converged on you and one other suspect, and you could vote independently or help tie the ballot. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed roles and cleared players are public and some evil is already dead, leaving a small unverified pool. Little direct evidence separates the people in that pool. Stakes: With few players left, losing a town-aligned player with bullets, or giving a necromancer a usable body, can swing the endgame. Surviving the vote through a tie keeps the shot for the night. Consensus: The village is largely aligned on narrowing the remaining evil to the few unverified players. Verified roles and dead wolves or killers drive this, and you are one of the targets. My position: holding out Heat: High to critical: claimed utility roles named you, or investigation cleared others and left you in the shrinking unverified pool. Forward exposure: A lone vote on a third party is public and permanent. If the wagon on you is larger, you are eliminated and your body, with its shots, becomes usable by a necromancer. Voting with the other suspect's pile can tie the ballot and is a low-cost, sincere-looking vote. Target landscape: The candidates are yourself (unverified, under pressure), one other unaligned or unverified suspect already drawing votes, and a quiet third player. Suspicion rests on behavior and elimination of the verified pool rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately you are town with unspent bullets; publicly utility-role claimants and the room treat you as a leading suspect for the remaining evil, such as the necromancer or last wolf.

action: If a majority is forming on you and you hold bullets, use your last word before the vote to state plainly that you are the vigilante and how many shots remain. Then vote for your sincere top suspect among the unverified players and invite the town to confirm your role by the reading of your record if you die. A claim stops a wagon only if the room finds it credible, so use it when you are the clear leading target.
situation: The village is closing on the vigilante at the day vote, after an investigation cleared others and left the unclaimed vigilante as the leading wolf candidate. Information landscape: Information-rich: investigation clearances, dead killers or wolves, and role claims leave a very small pool. There is no direct evidence against the vigilante, only exclusion. Stakes: One more town loss may let the remaining evil reach parity. Dying silent with shots unspent wastes the town's proactive attack, while a credible claim may stop the wagon or leave the town with usable information. Consensus: The village has consolidated on the unclaimed player by process of elimination, with a large majority and few dissenters. My position: holding out Heat: Critical: you are the prime elimination target because others have been cleared or have claimed roles and you have not. Forward exposure: Claiming reveals a bullet-holding town role to wolves and killers, which is a cost, but you are already near elimination. It cannot be taken back. If you are eliminated anyway, your role is revealed and the town can act on it, and a hidden role would give them nothing. Target landscape: The pool is a few unverified players: a role-exhausted or unconfirmed player, a suspected evil player, and you. The village majority is moving on you because you are unclaimed. Public vs private: You privately know you are a town vigilante with shots in hand. The room has no confirmation of this and treats your silence as evidence of evil.

action: At four alive, before casting the deciding vote, test each accusation against the rule text. A claim that matches the rules, such as a Sentinel's own watch not appearing in its result, is not wolf evidence. Vote the player whose claim actually conflicts with the rules or with confirmed wills and morning reports, or who has an evidence-based tell, rather than someone who merely sounds off.
situation: Four players remain with one wolf left in the endgame. Two claimed investigators-type roles contradict each other over how night mechanics work, and the vigilante's vote decides the day. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles and wills are confirmed. It is distorted by an uncontested fake claim and by players misstating visit rules. Stakes: One wrong vote leaves three players alive and lets the wolf reach parity with the next night kill. The vote is effectively the whole game. Consensus: The village is split or deadlocked between conflicting claims, and no side has a clear evidence-based majority. My position: driving Heat: Moderate. Players pressed you to reveal your role, and the pressure eased once you claimed vigilante and explained your shot. Forward exposure: A deciding vote on a claimed role is irreversible. A wrong elimination leaves three players alive with no margin for error, and if you are already revealed you are exposed to the night kill. Target landscape: The candidates are two or three players, some with competing role claims (e.g. a claimed Sentinel versus a claimed Trailseer) and one unclaimed. The basis is mostly claim contradictions and mechanical statements rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: You know your own vigilante status and bullet count. Beyond that, the room is deadlocked on conflicting night-action claims and you have no private evidence on who the wolf is.

action: When one wolf remains with no lone killer, your innocence is confirmed and you know the target pool, so vote the unverified player with the most concrete evidence against them. Good evidence is dodging a sigil trap or opposing confirmed or concealed information roles. Join the majority and commit the deciding vote, since a miss concedes the game anyway.
situation: Four players remain after the Investigator's death, with the Serial Killer and Chanteuse already eliminated. The village must find the lone remaining wolf among two unverified players to avoid defeat. Information landscape: Information-rich: earlier eliminations are confirmed, the Investigator's will clears you, and the sigil's non-trigger narrowed the pool. Stakes: Eliminating the last wolf ends the game with a town win. A miss leaves three alive and gives the wolf parity at night. Consensus: Most of the village, including the claimed sigilist and the neutral voter, is converging on the same suspect based on their behavior toward information roles. My position: with majority Heat: Zero. A dead Investigator's will publicly cleared you. Forward exposure: A visible vote on the suspect costs nothing, because you are already cleared. It is irreversible, and a miss at this count concedes the game. Target landscape: Two unverified players remain. One avoided the sigilist's trap and opposed the concealed tracker, and the other is low-profile with cautious votes. The basis is behavior and sigil non-triggers rather than hard confirmation. Public vs private: Your innocence is publicly confirmed by a dead Investigator's will, and privately you hold an unused bullet. Public and private views agree you are town.

action: When you still hold bullets and the information is rich (verified claims, dead roles revealed), cast your day vote with the verified town information core on the player their evidence points to, rather than going out on your own. If you are being targeted, the vote is the moment to protect your life, because a dead vigilante's body can be used by a Necromancer.
situation: Mid-game vote with several town roles and at least one evil faction dead or revealed, bodies concealed or revealed, and the village split between two or three candidate suspects. The vigilante, with bullets in hand, must choose a vote that does not isolate them. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles revealed, an investigator or sentinel claim, a concealed casualty, and visible voting records, yet no decisive proof against any one candidate. Stakes: With about six or seven alive and two evil factions active, each vote can swing the balance toward parity. Losing the vigilante with bullets unspent wastes town firepower and can hand a Necromancer a usable body. Consensus: The room is split between a verified town information core and a loose group of unconfirmed players. It is aligned on the dead wolf's death and the revealed roles, but not on who to eliminate next. My position: holding_out Heat: Ranges from low, when an investigator publicly cleared me, to extremely high, when five players suddenly voted me with no prior accusation. Heat can appear abruptly at the vote even when the morning discussion held no accusations. Forward exposure: A vote aligned with the verified core commits me only to a read the room can see, and it hides my vigilante role. A lone dissenting vote on an unconfirmed player is public and permanent, and it leaves me outside the town bloc that could defend me. Target landscape: Candidates are an unconfirmed player with subtle behavioral signs, such as probing a dead town claimant's findings, and a quiet player pushed by a dead wolf's vote. The verified town claims (investigator, sentinel, sigilist) are not themselves suspects, and the choice rests on thin behavior rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately hold unspent lethal bullets and know I am town, while the public read of me ranges from cleared by an investigator claim to suddenly targeted without any open accusation.

action: When evil is narrowed to a small pool and you still hold bullets, shoot the most probable evil candidate instead of holding fire. Pick the one the evidence leaves most suspect: a quiet unvetted player when public clears and saves have eliminated the rest, or an unconfirmed player when a lone killer is still attacking. Unspent bullets are worth nothing if you are voted out or the town margin shrinks first.
situation: Late-mid game with few players alive, wolves or other evil killers still active, and the unresolved suspect pool down to two or three players, possibly including the vigilante itself. The vigilante still has bullets and is deciding whether to shoot or conserve. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich on cleared and claimed town roles from checks, saves, and claims. Information-starved on which of the remaining quiet players is the actual killer. Stakes: The board is near parity, so each night an evil killer stays alive moves the town closer to losing. A correct shot can remove the last killer or wolf outright. Holding fire risks a day-vote mis-elimination of the vigilante itself with every bullet unused. Forward exposure: Shooting spends a bullet permanently and is irreversible. A miss kills an innocent unconfirmed town role, but the shot is hidden from the town unless it kills. Holding fire keeps the bullet but leaves the vigilante unverified and exposed to the day vote. Target landscape: Two or three unconfirmed quiet players remain among a mostly cleared or role-claimed board. Power roles (investigator, healer, sentinel, trailseer) are publicly claimed or cleared. The evil pool is narrowed by elimination and checks, not by hard proof on any single player.

action: When confirmed facts (a revealed role, a disproven counter-claim, or a timeline contradiction a night-info role has reported) point to a specific living player as a wolf, spend one of your bullets on that player rather than holding fire. If two or more players fit, shoot the one whose story is mechanically impossible or the one a day vote could not remove (tie or no elimination).
situation: Mid-game after a day vote that either mis-eliminated a Town role or deadlocked in a tie. Wolves are still alive, and one specific player is exposed by confirmed role information or a contradiction. Information landscape: Information-rich: a game-master role reveal or a claimed night-info result contradicts a rival claimant or accused player's story, giving a concrete lead. Stakes: The board is close to parity, so one wolf removed by a night shot can decide the game. Removing a wolf cuts the pack's kill power and its abilities, and in one case ended the wolf faction outright, leaving only the lone killer. Forward exposure: The shot is a visit and attack that spends a bullet permanently; the morning report announces a vigilante kill but not who fired, so your identity stays hidden. It cannot be undone, and a miss on a non-wolf costs a bullet and a Town life. Target landscape: A few candidates: a player whose claim was disproven by a role reveal or whose defense rests on flawed timing, versus unverified passive players and already-claimed Town roles. The leading target is chosen on hard evidence (confirmed reveal, contradiction), not on mere behavior.

action: With your last bullet, three or four players alive and one evil player left, fire the shot tonight instead of holding it. A wolf kill or a Necromancer kill ends the game on the spot, so a held bullet is usually never used, and a shot is the only way town can remove the killer first.
situation: Endgame at about three players alive. The last evil faction needs just one more death for parity, and the vigilante holds the only remaining offensive tool. Information landscape: Information-rich: earlier eliminations have revealed roles, and vote and claim records are on file, but the last evil player is not yet proven. Stakes: The next night death hands the evil side parity or a win, so holding the bullet gains nothing. One correct shot wins the game at once, and one wrong shot loses it. Forward exposure: Spends the last bullet and cannot be undone. Your vigilante claim is already public, so the killer expects a shot or an attack on you. Holding fire leaves your role and bullet exposed to the night kill. Target landscape: Two or three survivors, one of them the last evil player. Some have claimed roles that are confirmed or contradicted by announced reveals. The rest are quiet or unclaimed.

action: When no role has been confirmed and no night result or vote record singles anyone out, hold fire and keep your bullets for a lead that actually names someone, such as an investigator's Suspicious result, a caught lie, or a flipped wolf's defenders. A shot is an attack that spends a bullet even if it misses or hits an immune player, so a blind shot is mostly friendly fire.
situation: Opening or early night with no eliminations or only a few deaths, no verified evil leads, and conflicting or unverifiable claims. The vigilante must decide whether to shoot blind or hold fire. Information landscape: Information-starved: no investigation results are public, there is no voting history that separates town from evil, and claims are unverified. Any lead is speculation. Stakes: Evil is far from parity, so there is time to wait for evidence. A wasted bullet or a dead power role costs more than waiting one more night. The risk is dying with unused bullets, which is acceptable early but should push you to fire once a real lead appears. Forward exposure: A shot spends one of very few non-renewable bullets and is a visible attack in the morning report, so it cannot be undone. Holding fire commits to nothing and leaves both the shot and your identity available for a better-informed night. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no public role confirmations. Alignments are unknown, and the only basis for a read is thin behavior such as abstentions or a minority vote, not evidence. The pool may include a night-immune serial killer or town power roles.
